summary: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.
title: SlideRule

summary: Background: Surface roughness is an important characteristic of resin composite restorations and may be influenced by material composition and finishing and polishing procedures. Objective: To evaluate changes in surface roughness (Ra) of nanofilled, nanohybrid, and microhybrid resin composites after sequential finishing and polishing and to compare their final surface roughness. Materials and Methods: S ixty disc-shaped specimens (8 mm × 2 mm; shade A2) were fabricated using Filtek Z350 XT, IPS Empress Direct, and Filtek Z250 (n = 20 per material). Fifteen specimens per material underwent a standardized finishing and polishing protocol using fine- and extra-fine-grit diamond burs followed by sequential Sof-Lex discs, while five specimens per material remained untreated as controls. Surface roughness was measured using a Mitutoyo SJ-210 contact profilometer at baseline   and after the intervention. Because specimen-level identification was not preserved between measurement sessions, baseline and final measurements were analyzed as independent observations using independent-samples t-tests, with Welch’s correction when required. Final Ra values among materials were compared using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey HSD tests (α = 0.05). Results: All three experimental composites showed statistically significant increases in Ra after finishing and polishing (all p < 0.001), whereas no statistically significant changes were observed in the untreated controls (all p > 0.05). Mean Ra increased from 0.085 to 0.181 μm for IPS Empress Direct, from 0.111 to 0.186 μm for Filtek Z350 XT, and from 0.122 to 0.195 μm for Filtek Z250. Final Ra values did not differ significantly among the three materials (F(2,42) = 0.559, p = 0.576). Conclusions: Sequential finishing and polishing significantly increased surface roughness relative to the strip-polymerized baseline surfaces of all three resin composites, without statistically significant differences in final Ra among the materials. The final mean Ra values remained below the predefined 0.2 μm surface-roughness threshold. Under the experimental conditions evaluated, post-polishing surface roughness could not be predicted solely on the basis of nanofilled, nanohybrid, or microhybrid filler classification.
title: Surface Roughness of Nanofilled, Nanohybrid, and Microhy-brid Resin Composites After Sequential Finishing and Polish-ing: An In Vitro Comparative Study

summary: This deposit contains the results replication package for the article “Governing the Eurasian Roundabout: Anti-Circumvention Governance and Post-Soviet Intermediaries after 2022.” It reconstructs the article’s quantitative trade evidence from archived Eurostat Easy Comext data and provides structured versions of all numbered tables and figures. The product-specific analysis covers monthly EU27 exports from January 2019 through December 2025 for the 50 six-digit Harmonized System codes in the February 2024 Common High Priority Items list and 13 destinations. The workflow constructs the balanced product–partner–month panel, aggregates partner–month exports, calculates raw and normalized summaries, compares product-specific growth with total-export growth, estimates descriptive partner- and month-fixed-effects paths, and reproduces the reported comparison windows and sensitivity checks. The reconstructed evidence shows a sharp contraction in mean monthly EU exports of Common High Priority Items to Russia, from EUR 295.7 million in 2021 to EUR 3.3 million in 2023–2025, alongside increases from EUR 13.934 million to EUR 30.835 million for Kazakhstan and from EUR 1.319 million to EUR 4.496 million for Armenia. Product-specific export growth exceeded total-export growth in both focal destinations, by 14.1 index points in Kazakhstan and 74.2 index points in Armenia. The package also reproduces the pre-event diagnostic, late-2021 contrast, alternative normalizations, product and comparison-set checks, alternative windows, destination distribution, and descriptive policy-milestone summaries. These results are descriptive and corroborative. They do not identify onward shipment, circumvention, ultimate buyers or end users, enforcement effectiveness, or causal policy effects. The archived product-specific and total-export series come from different Eurostat data vintages, and the broad comparison is interpreted accordingly. Run the complete analysis from the extracted package directory with one command: python3 reproduce.py This deposit is associated with the results package at https://zenodo.org/records/19206576 that supports former version of the article.
title: Governing the Eurasian Roundabout: Anti-Circumvention Governance and Post-Soviet Intermediaries after 2022. V2

summary: Electric vehicles (EVs) experience significant  driving  range degradation in low ambient temperature conditions, primarily due to the elevated energy demand of heating system.  T his paper proposes  an optimal  control strategy for a  positive temperature coefficient ( PTC )  heater-based electric minibus  heating system ,  which is  aimed to  exploit actuators’ redundancy for  energy consumption  minimization  and driving range extension . The strategy  optimally  allocates  control inputs  of multiple actuators  to  provide  heating power demand ed  by a superimposed proportional-integral (PI)  feedback  controller of the  passenger  cabin air temperatur e .  The  optimal  allocation maps prescri be  coolant pump flow, blower air   flow, and inlet air temperature references , and they  are obtained by comprehensive simulations of a high-fidelity multi-physics heating system model over a wide range of quasi-stationary operating conditions .   A low-level PI controller is further designed for the full ,  allocation-related range of operating points to track the  allocated  inlet air temperature reference, while commanding the PTC heater power.   The overall control strategy is validated through co-simulation with a high-fidelity vehicle model  in comparison with an industry baseline strategy , demonstrating a considerable energy consumption reduction in both quasi-stationary and transient (heat up) conditions, as well as improved control performance in terms of shorter heat up intervals.
title: Optimal Control Allocation Strategy for an Energy-efficient PTC Heater-based Electric Vehicle Passenger Cabin Heating System

summary: Abstract Background  Thyroid dysfunction is one of the most common endocrine disorders affecting metabolic activity, psychological well-being, and gastrointestinal function.(1,2) Patients frequently experience elevated thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) levels, stress, bloating, impaired digestion, reduced metabolic efficiency, and decreased quality of life. Although conventional treatment effectively restores thyroid hormone balance in many patients, complementary therapeutic interventions are increasingly being explored to improve overall clinical outcomes and patient-reported health status.  Aim  To evaluate the effect of a Teacurry Thyro Herb Tea for Thyroid on thyroid function, perceived stress, gastrointestinal symptoms, and participant-reported global improvement among adults with thyroid dysfunction.  Materials and Methods:  A prospective, single-arm interventional clinical study was conducted involving  22 adult participants  diagnosed with thyroid dysfunction. Baseline demographic characteristics including age, body weight, height, and body mass index (BMI) were recorded. Clinical assessments included serum thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), perceived stress score (0–40 scale), gastrointestinal symptoms related to bloating, digestion, and metabolism, and Participant Global Impression of Change (PGIC). All parameters were assessed before and after the intervention. The composition of the study formulation will be described separately. Statistical analysis was performed using appropriate descriptive and inferential statistical methods, and statistical significance was considered at  p  < 0.05.  Results:  The intervention demonstrated an overall improvement in multiple clinical outcomes. Mean serum TSH decreased from  10.27 to 3.77 mIU/L , while mean perceived stress scores decreased from  20.45 to 13.18 . Improvement in gastrointestinal symptoms and PGIC scores was observed in the majority of participants. Perceived stress scores decreased in a substantial proportion of participants, indicating improvement in psychological well-being. Gastrointestinal symptoms such as bloating and impaired digestion improved from mild or moderate severity to normal or minimal symptoms in the majority of cases. Participant-reported outcomes also demonstrated favorable changes, with PGIC scores increasing in most participants, suggesting meaningful overall clinical improvement. The intervention was generally well tolerated, and no serious adverse events were documented during the study period.  Conclusion:  The findings of this prospective clinical study suggest that the investigated Teacurry Thyro Herb Tea for Thyroid may contribute to improved thyroid function, reduction in perceived stress, better gastrointestinal health, and enhanced patient-reported quality of life in adults with thyroid dysfunction. These preliminary findings support the potential role of the formulation as a complementary therapeutic option. Larger randomized controlled clinical trials with extended follow-up are warranted to confirm these observations and establish long-term efficacy and safety.   Keywords: Thyroid Dysfunction; Thyroid Stimulating Hormone; TSH; Teacurry Thyro Herb Tea for Thyroid; Teacurry Thyroid Tea; Teacurry; Thyroid Tea; Herbal Tea for Thyroid; Complementary ##plugin
title: Effect of a Plant-Based Herbal Tea Formulation "Teacurry Thyro Herb Tea for Thyroid" on Thyroid Function, TSH Levels, Gastrointestinal Symptoms and Participant-Reported Global Improvement in Adults with Thyroid Dysfunction: Real-World Evidence Clinical Study

The manuscript was rejected by Journal of Molecular Evolution on 9 September 2026; the reviewer's comment on the imposed species-tree topology prompted the re-analysis. (The README inside the archive calls 10.5281/zenodo.21094823 the concept DOI; that number denotes version 1.) Re-analysis (11 September 2026) identified: a rooted-tree input to PAML codeml that made root-adjacent branch estimates non-identifiable and inflated the headline statistic (88.6 % → 71.5 % with unrooted trees; 845 → 1,374 orthogroups after QC); imposed species and gene-tree topologies that are rejected by the data themselves (Astrephomene is sister to Volvocaceae, support 100/100); pooling of two independent origins of multicellularity that carry different results (Goniaceae+Volvocaceae 73 %, Tetrabaenaceae 48 %); and a terminal-branch-length gradient that confounds evolutionary rate with time since each lineage's last sampled split (differentiated lineages are not slower than their undifferentiated sister clades in 263 public genes, and there is no cell-number gradient across 57 species: PGLS β = −0.04, P = 0.69). Supplementary Tables S5b/S5c contained unfinished placeholders. The original summary statistics and interpretations in Figures 1, 2, 3, S1, S2 and Tables S2–S5 should not be relied upon; they are retained unchanged for audit only. The orthogroup table, gene predictions and the per-orthogroup codon/amino-acid alignments inside the archives remain valid; the trees and omega estimates in them do not (rooted trees; -te topology constraints). * figures/, supplementary/, summary_tables/, scripts/ — unchanged from version 1 and from the never-published July 2026 package, historical, unreliable as documented in the manifest and README. * README.md — full description, headline-statement status table, reproduction instructions. summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. Version numbers allow researchers to confirm their data has all been processed in a compati

summary: L'Ange des projections lumineuses was a monthly journal published for the Œuvre des projections catéchistiques of Champtercier (Basses-Alpes), printed at Lyon, and edited by the abbé Georges Aillaud. It ran from 15 October 1902 to 15 September 1903 as the organ of a subscription lending library that circulated magic-lantern slide sets to village clergy, together with the technical advice, lecture texts and equipment notices needed to use them. This deposit is a complete transcription of the ten issues held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France — 198 pages. Numbers 10 and 11, July and August 1903, are absent from the BnF holdings and no copies have been located elsewhere. The journal documents a working provincial distribution network at the moment cinema was arriving in rural France: it lists the slide sets in circulation and their prices, reports what was shown and where, argues over illuminants and apparatus, and by its final number is advertising a cinematograph alongside the lantern equipment. Its technical columns are a detailed record of alcohol, Auer and acetylene illumination in non-commercial exhibition. Method. The text was read from the BnF's page images by a vision language model working on overlapping half-page tiles, without optical character recognition, and then compared word by word by machine against the BnF's own OCR text layer wherever one exists. 1,864 disagreements were found across the 150 pages with a text layer, classified automatically, and checked selectively — not exhaustively — against the page images; eight readings were corrected as a result, and a separate audit for digital artefacts produced a further fifty. Every correction is logged with its evidence. This is machine transcription with editorial checking: it has not been proofread cover to cover against the original and should not be described as though it had. The February, March and April 1903 issues have no BnF text layer, rest on a single reading, and are identified as such. Spelling, accentuation, capitalisation and punctuation follow the page, including where the printing is inconsistent with itself. Contents of this deposit. The reading edition as PDF (119 pp.) and as plain UTF-8 text, both carrying the editorial note as front matter; the per-page source files, which preserve the printed line breaks and their end-of-line hyphens, with the flags raised on each page and a separate folder for the eighteen non-journal leaves; the editorial note; an apparatus of 137 unresolved or adjudicated readings; the full correction log; and the complete uncurated production log, labelled as provenance documentation rather than an apparatus. See README.md. Source. Bibliothèque nationale de France, shelfmark D-72088 (BIS); ISSN 2273-6220; BnF catalogue record cb326930724. Page images: Source gallica.bnf.fr / Bibliothèque nationale de France . Rights. The journal text is in the public domain. The editorial note, annotations, arrangement and other original editorial contributions are licensed under CC BY 4.0 . No copyright is asserted over the underlying public-domain text. Related. A prose introduction to the journal — its publisher, the slide network it served, and its bearing on the arrival of cinema in provincial France — was published at the time of this deposit at billlefurgy.com/ange-des-projections-lumineuses . It is not part of this deposit and is not covered by the method statement above.

summary: L'Ange des projections lumineuses was a monthly journal published for the Œuvre des projections catéchistiques of Champtercier (Basses-Alpes), printed at Lyon, and edited by the abbé Georges Aillaud. It ran from 15 October 1902 to 15 September 1903 as the organ of a subscription lending library that circulated magic-lantern slide sets to village clergy, together with the technical advice, lecture texts and equipment notices needed to use them. This deposit is a complete transcription of the ten issues held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France — 198 pages. Numbers 10 and 11, July and August 1903, are absent from the BnF holdings and no copies have been located elsewhere. The journal documents a working provincial distribution network at the moment cinema was arriving in rural France: it lists the slide sets in circulation and their prices, reports what was shown and where, argues over illuminants and apparatus, and by its final number is advertising a cinematograph alongside the lantern equipment. Its technical columns are a detailed record of alcohol, Auer and acetylene illumination in non-commercial exhibition. Method. The text was read from the BnF's page images by a vision language model working on overlapping half-page tiles, without optical character recognition, and then compared word by word by machine against the BnF's own OCR text layer wherever one exists. 1,864 disagreements were found across the 150 pages with a text layer, classified automatically, and checked selectively — not exhaustively — against the page images; eight readings were corrected as a result, and a separate audit for digital artefacts produced a further fifty. Every correction is logged with its evidence. This is machine transcription with editorial checking: it has not been proofread cover to cover against the original and should not be described as though it had. The February, March and April 1903 issues have no BnF text layer, rest on a single reading, and are identified as such. Spelling, accentuation, capitalisation and punctuation follow the page, including where the printing is inconsistent with itself. Contents of this deposit. The reading edition as PDF (119 pp.) and as plain UTF-8 text, both carrying the editorial note as front matter; the per-page source files, which preserve the printed line breaks and their end-of-line hyphens, with the flags raised on each page and a separate folder for the eighteen non-journal leaves; the editorial note; an apparatus of 137 unresolved or adjudicated readings; the full correction log; and the complete uncurated production log, labelled as provenance documentation rather than an apparatus. See README.md. Source. Bibliothèque nationale de France, shelfmark D-72088 (BIS); ISSN 2273-6220; BnF catalogue record cb326930724. summary: Per-pixel  active-flame  image–mask chips from  Sentinel-2  covering  25 large California wildfires  (acquisitions spanning 2020–2026). The deposit contains  2,148  co-registered pairs of false-colour composites and segmentation masks. Each chip is  512 × 512 pixels at 20 m  (~10.24 km across), rendered as a fixed-stretch RGB composite ( R = B12 / SWIR2 ,  G = B11 / SWIR1 ,  B = B8A / NIR ) so flaming combustion is separable from cloud, smoke, fresh char, and bright reflective surfaces. Masks were generated automatically with a  modified HOTMAP SWIR hotspot rule  (confirmed flame where B12 and B12/B8A exceed conservative thresholds, plus a connected growth tier for cooler front margins). Pixel values are  0 = background ,  1 = active fire , and  255 = no-data  (outside the acquisition footprint). The corpus uses a  leak-free fire holdout : whole incidents are assigned to partitions ( 18 train / 3 validation / 4 test ), so evaluation measures transfer to unseen fires rather than random chips from the same landscape. This archive includes: images/  and  masks/  (2,148 PNG files each) summary.csv  (chip-level metadata) partitions.csv  (fire → split assignment) analyst_review/hand_masks/  ( 233  independently reviewed test chips;  54%  of the test split), for quantifying weak-label agreement at chip/cluster level Companion  code , labelling protocol, baseline training scripts, and manuscript figures are available at:   https://github.com/MohammadrezaNarimaniUCDavis/California_Sentinel2_Active_Fire_Dataset This dataset supports a data article prepared for submission to  Data in Brief (Elsevier).
title: California Sentinel-2 Active-Fire Segmentation Dataset

summary: Calibration release: the package's no-shipped-coefficients policy finally comes with the tool that closes the loop. Every shipped set carries the caveat that lever arms depend on material, mode pair, excitation and substrate; calibrate_lever_arms turns reference measurements you control -- a strain-stage sweep, a gated sweep, any points with known (strain, density) -- into your own fitted coefficient matrix, with uncertainties and provenance. New in ramansep.calibration calibrate_lever_arms : weighted least-squares fit of the (m, 2) lever-arm matrix, one linear problem per mode on the shared reference design. With shift sigmas the parameter covariance is the exact known-noise Gauss-Markov result and a per-mode chi-square consistency check comes back with it; without sigmas the covariance uses the residual variance, which is why that path refuses fewer than three reference points instead of inventing an error bar. Identifiability refused, not fudged : reference states collinear in the (strain, density) plane (a strain-only sweep, or gating that strains proportionally) cannot separately determine the two arms of any mode -- the fit raises with an explanation instead of returning one of infinitely many minimizers. CalibrationResult.coefficients() packages a two-mode calibration as a ModeCoefficients with a MANDATORY provenance string; result.K feeds MultiModeModel directly for m > 2. Anchors (asserted in the tests, not stated) Noise-free shifts from a known matrix are recovered to machine precision, with zero estimated uncertainty. The hand-built normal-equation solution agrees with an independent QR solve ( numpy.linalg.lstsq on the whitened system) to 1e-10. The orthogonal unit design {(1,0), (0,1)} with unit sigmas has EXACTLY the identity parameter covariance -- the closed form, not an approximation. Seeded Monte-Carlo scatter of the fitted arms matches the reported sigmas. Degenerate and malformed reference sets raise (collinear designs, n = 1, n = 2 without sigmas, non-positive sigmas, non-finite shifts). The full round trip -- calibrate on synthetic references, package the coefficients, invert forward-generated maps through SeparationModel -- returns the input strain and density maps to 1e-10. 50 tests across Python 3.9-3.13. Install: pip install -U ramansep .
title: ramansep: two-mode separation of strain and carrier density in 2D-material Raman maps

summary: Code obfuscation is the conversion of original source code into a functionally equivalent but less readable form, aiming to prevent reverse engineering and intellectual property theft. This is a challenging task since it is crucial to maintain functional correctness of the code while substantially disguising the input code. The recent development of large language models (LLMs) paves the way for practical applications in different domains, including software engineering. This work performs an empirical study on the ability of LLMs to obfuscate Python source code and introduces a metric (i.e., semantic elasticity) to measure the quality degree of obfuscated code. We experimented with 3 leading LLMs, i.e., Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5, GPT-4-Turbo across 30 Python functions from diverse computational domains. Our findings reveal GPT-4-Turbo’s remarkable effectiveness with few-shot prompting (81% pass rate versus 29% standard prompting), significantly outperforming both Gemini-1.5 (39%) and Claude-3.5-Sonnet (30%). Notably, we discovered a counter-intuitive “obfuscation by simplification” phenomenon where models consistently reduce rather than increase cyclomatic complexity. This study provides a methodological framework for evaluating AI-driven obfuscation while highlighting promising directions for leveraging LLMs in software security.
title: Simplicity by Obfuscation: Evaluating LLM-Driven Code Transformation with Semantic Elasticity

summary: Python package and command-line tool that estimates the share of variance in an antimicrobial resistance phenotype carried by the lineages of a bacterial collection, from a lineage label and a susceptibility call or a recorded dilution, and refuses the estimate where the collection cannot support one. One collection admits three quantities and the package reports them apart: the lineage-membership share, what a rule scored out of sample reaches, with a lineage bootstrap; the design-corrected component ratio of the same collection, with an interval exact under the Gaussian one-way model by inversion of a noncentral F; and the superpopulation share for the species, with a chi-square layer on the number of lineages. Each is scored against its own truth on 135 simulated cells from five lineages to a thousand, and each sits behind a gate that refuses where the collection cannot identify the quantity or the residuals contradict the law the interval assumes, the coverage of each having been measured. A binary share is restated on the latent scale of the threshold model beside the observed scale. The lineage label may be a sequence type, a core-genome or SNP cluster, or a serovar, so the same estimate can be read at two typing resolutions. For a difference in non-wild-type prevalence between two collections it applies the Kitagawa decomposition to split the difference into a lineage-composition component and a within-lineage rate component, with a shared-support gate calibrated against measured interval coverage, a test for lineage labels that are differentially and informatively missing, and Benjamini-Yekutieli control within each component family of the antimicrobial panel, valid whatever the dependence between agents. Ships a Streptococcus suis case study (677 isolates, 650 porcine and 27 human, with full data provenance) read at population-cluster and at sequence-type resolution, together with a 720,000-decomposition calibration study and a head-to-head comparison against lineage-adjusted logistic regression. The package reads two tables and never a genome. A susceptibility panel is read at its recorded resolution: a dichotomised call and a recorded dilution are both intervals on the log2 concentration scale and enter one interval likelihood, so the input mode changes how much an observation carries rather than what is estimated. The interval is exact where every reading is a point and calibrated by simulation where a reading is an interval, and the tested wells are taken from the recorded values unless the panel is supplied. Each share carries an e-value; a run that declares the intake each isolate arrived in also carries the running product over intakes, a test supermartingale that may be read after any intake, with the panel decision taken on the log scale so that evidence too strong for a float is still evidence. False-discovery control across the panel holds under arbitrary dependence. The attribution is exercised outside the shipped cohorts on fifty organisms of one NCBI Pathogen Detection release, each taken at the release accession the retrieval recorded: every agent of every cohort that reaches the estimator leaves one record, estimated or refused with the condition that failed, 192 cells are estimated in twelve species and 44 admitted by the support gate in six, and every cell carries a permuted-label control. The Streptococcus suis cohort is read at three definitions of a lineage, population cluster, serotype and sequence type, with the reference label rerun on each other label's own isolates so that the label is separated from the collection. A veterinary arm cuts the same source by host species and by sampling matrix and runs every cell at two definitions of a lineage, the Pathogen Detection SNP cluster and the serovar, with the permuted-label control at both. The pair is reported rather than one number, because the share a cohort carries is a function of the resolution at which a lineage is defined, and a laboratory
title: amr-clonalshare: measuring how much of antimicrobial resistance travels with the clone

summary: Version 1.3.0 accompanies Hongru Zhao’s manuscript, Uniform Hiding and Two Routes to Relative Accuracy in Gaussian Boson Sampling. It extends the formalization of the hiding result and Route 1 with photon-sector calculations, optimized asymptotics, sampling bounds, and applications. Changes in version 1.3.0 Current manuscript correspondence: the release now accounts for all 178 labeled equations and 15 named mathematical results in the current 49-page hiding paper. The table distinguishes proved statements and consequences, definitions, imported inputs, sampler assumptions, and the external Route 2 comparison. It uses the current compiled equation numbers and records the exact manuscript source fingerprints. Twenty-three new equation checks identify the actual gradient in (D.2), verify all expanded moments and both coefficient arrays in (F.3) and Table 3, check the variance identity (D.41), retain the expectation-level Taylor form of (D.62), and verify the boundary exponent, power integral, and displayed constant arithmetic. No project axiom is added. Appendix E was also checked again. The fresh audit covers 281 declarations. Every new equation check and every Appendix E endpoint uses only Lean's standard foundations. Appendix E: a dedicated equation-level supplement now verifies (E.1)–(E.12), the twelve numbered displays in the proof of Lemma 6.5. It checks the finite normalizer, the density ratio and its strict support, the exact KL expectation identity, the log-determinant estimate, the Haar fourth-entry formula, the two Gram moments, the cancellation, and the Pinsker bounds. Twenty-three equation endpoints passed a fresh Lean check and transitive axiom audit. Each uses only Lean’s standard foundations; no project axiom was added. The supplement includes the equation mapping and execution receipt. Proposition 4.1: the development now constructs the normalized single-mode photon-pair probability law, convolves independent squeezed inputs, proves the generating function and even/odd photon-count probabilities, and proves photon-number conservation under the passive tensor action. The output-sector probability and reference-scale identity no longer require the earlier premise supplying the total-photon formula. The maximizing squeezing parameter, a uniform Stirling bound for both integer and half-integer Gamma arguments, and the final inverse-square-root reference-scale asymptotics are proved. Corollary 3.3: the optimized Route 1 public bound is proved to tend to zero under the manuscript’s hypotheses. Corollary 4.2: the average-total-variation sampling bound, including zero sampling error and its square-root optimization, is proved for Route 1. Proposition G.2: the independent-product, maximum-CDF, and binomial-count transfers now cover the full positive input range, including fewer inputs than selected rows. The coverage report also corrects an earlier omission: Lemma 6.2’s signed-measure contraction and derivative transport were already formalized. Their dependency sets have been rechecked; these are retained proofs, not new ones. The all-input Theorem 2.1 and its immediate Corollary 2.2 are retained from the version 1.2.0 source update. They include the quantitative product-hiding specialization corresponding to Ehrenberg et al., Conjecture 1 (Formal), Supplemental Eq. (S62). Connection with GitHub Development is maintained in UniformHiding . The archive’s UniformHiding directory matches the GitHub source snapshot for version 1.3.0 . Both contain the same 893 Lean source files. Zenodo additionally includes the Appendix E equation checks, the complete current-paper correspondence and its equation supplement, and historical verification records. Historical records retain their original dates and source snapshots. Route 1 uses the companion Gaussian anticoncentration theorem and its dependencies from the companion ComplexGramHafnians source version used in this release . All 225 included co
title: Lean Verification for "Uniform Hiding and Two Routes to Relative Accuracy in Gaussian Boson Sampling"

summary: This dataset accompanies “Population-scale burden analysis of rare damaging coding variants identifies novel risk genes for Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias and Parkinson’s disease and related disorders” by Le Guen, Peña-Tauber and colleagues. The release contains 16 gzip-compressed, tab-delimited gene-based burden summary-statistic files covering Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), and Parkinson’s disease and related disorders (PDRD); combined-proxy and direct-diagnosis ascertainment; and all-ancestry (ALL) and European-ancestry (EUR) analyses. The files share 61 columns and contain 1,000,189 retained gene/mask analysis rows in total, including nonsignificant results. The four nested masks comprise high-confidence loss-of-function variants alone or together with qualifying missense variants at REVEL thresholds of 0.75, 0.50 or 0.25. The associated manuscript specifies GRCh38 coordinates. The primary discovery analyses are AD combined-proxy ALL and PD combined-proxy ALL. EUR analyses are secondary ancestry analyses; AD-direct and PD-direct are secondary, nested phenotype-sensitivity analyses. All ADRD/PDRD analyses are diagnostic-sensitivity comparisons. Combined-proxy includes direct cases and family-history-only proxy cases, not proxy cases alone. Phenotype definitions and ancestry strata overlap and are not independent replication datasets. The release explicitly separates effect estimation from association evidence. REGENIE-only effect estimates combine compatible binary-outcome burden models from UK Biobank, All of Us and ADSP for AD/ADRD, or UK Biobank, All of Us and AMP-PD for PD/PDRD. Combined-proxy cohort effects use the revised exact common-control mixture-model inversion under kappa=0.5. ADES stage-1 estimates from Holstege et al. (2022) are reported separately because their ordinal summed-dosage model differs from the REGENIE binary-outcome maximum-allele burden model. Eligible ADES and REGENIE results are integrated through effective-sample-size-weighted signed-Z evidence; no ADES-inclusive pooled odds ratio is calculated. Use P_OVERALL or LOG10P_OVERALL for final association evidence, and the BETA_REGENIE, SE_REGENIE and REGENIE odds-ratio/confidence-interval columns for the pooled REGENIE effect estimate. AD/ADRD overall evidence falls back to REGENIE when eligible ADES evidence is unavailable. ADES does not contribute to PD/PDRD. The same ADES source is reused across AD-family comparisons and ancestry strata. The README and column dictionary define all fields, missing-value conventions, numerical precision and interpretation. A public manifest and checksums document all 16 files. The dataset contains aggregate gene-level results, not individual-level genotypes or single-variant summary statistics. Dataset DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22702628. License selected for this record: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).
title: Population-scale burden analysis of rare damaging coding variants identifies novel risk genes for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias and Parkinson's disease and related disorders

summary: Modern large language model research agents, commonly marketed under the label deep research, are highly capable at locating sources, verifying claims, and synthesizing existing literature into structured reports. This capability has not translated into a comparable capacity for scientific discovery. We argue that this gap has a specific, testable cause, which we call literature attracti on: the more strongly a generation process is grounded in retrieved literature, the more its outputs converge toward concepts already dominant in that literature, at the expense of novelty. We separate four quantities that are routinely conflated in evaluations of AI research systems: research depth, research novelty, research validity, and research value. We review the current frontier of deep research systems and automated science pipelines, describe the attention-level mechanisms that plausibly cause literature attraction in retrieval-augmented generation, and propose a controlled experimental protocol to measure the novelty-grounding tradeoff dir ectly, using embedding-based and graph-based novelty metrics, a temporal hold-out benchmark, and human expert validation. We then outline an architectural response: a two-stage exploit-then-explore pipeline in which a quality-diversity search process is used to deliberately push hypothesis generation into regions of the concept space that are underrepresented in the retrieved literature, while an adversarial falsification agent constrains the resulting hypotheses to remain scientificall y testable. We close with a proposed output format, the research novelty report, that reports where a generated hypothesis sits relative to existing knowledge rather than asserting that it is novel. This paper is a research proposal and experimental design; it does not claim to have already demonstrated the phenomenon it sets out to measure.
title: Escaping the Literature: Exploring New Scientific Ideas with Large Language Models

summary: This reproducibility package accompanies a measurement-science workflow for temporal light modulation (TLM) metric reproduction and computational sensitivity analysis. Five independent MK350S Premium optical waveform records form the bounded commercial demonstration. MetTLM W1–W20 public references support source-traceable PstLM/SVM calculation-pipeline reproduction and sampling-rate, duration and deterministic modelled-effect sensitivity analyses. Evidence identity is preserved so that public waveforms, resampled/windowed/perturbed rows and auxiliary electrical/photometric records are not treated as additional commercial observations. The package includes the five commercial raw waveform files, machine-readable commercial/context summaries, source code, public-reference provenance and checksums, frozen MetTLM reproduction outputs, sampling/duration/modelled-effect outputs, journal-neutral numerical and claim-boundary QC files and a journal-neutral manuscript snapshot. Raw third-party public-reference assets and manufacturer documents are intentionally not redistributed; original DOI/license/checksum provenance and reconstruction scripts are provided instead. The package supports calculation-pipeline reproduction and bounded commercial SVM-related screening. It does not constitute IEC certification, physical calibration, commercial-lamp PstLM, measurement uncertainty, commercial repeatability, PF–SVM causality or population-level generalization.
title: Reproducibility Package for Public-Reference Reproduction and Sensitivity Analysis of Temporal Light Modulation Metrics Using MetTLM

summary: This repository contains supplementary documentation for a qualitative interview study examining how Bachelor of Software Engineering students understand and use generative AI in their studies. The study investigates: (1) the roles students assign to generative AI and how these roles are enacted; (2) how generative AI transforms learning and software-development tasks and how students legitimize its adoption; and (3) how students negotiate and exercise agency when working with generative AI. The package includes: the interview guide and replication material; First Cycle codebooks organized by research question; Second Cycle Pattern Codes and explanations of their analytical development; a code-saturation monitoring record tracing code emergence, elaboration, and confirmation across interviews; and supplementary evidence tables supporting the reported findings. The interviews were analyzed using the two-cycle coding approach described by Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña. First Cycle coding combined descriptive, process, and values-oriented codes. During Second Cycle analysis, conceptually related First Cycle codes were synthesized into broader Pattern Codes. Interview recordings and full transcripts are not publicly available because they contain potentially identifying contextual information and were collected under confidentiality commitments. The package therefore supports analytical transparency and methodological replication without releasing the underlying confidential data. The materials should be interpreted in relation to the educational and institutional context reported in the associated publication. The codebooks and Pattern Codes represent an inductively developed analytical framework rather than a universal taxonomy of student AI adoption.
tags: Generative AI; Software Engineering Education; Student Agency; AI-Assisted Learning; Qualitative Research; Codebook; Pattern Coding; Code Saturation; Replication Package
title: Shared Documentation Package for "Learning with AI: How Software Engineering Students Enact AI Roles, Transform their Learning Practices, and Exercise Agency"

summary: Replication data and code for an analysis of how allocation procedures shape which Italian municipalities obtain Recovery and Resilience Facility resources, and whether they convert them into completed works. The package covers 68,990 projects implemented by municipal governments across 36 plan measures, extracted from the OpenPNRR REST API at the ReGiS extraction date of 13 June 2026. Each project carries a coded allocation regime — open window, competitive, administrative assignment, or decentralised regional selection — reconstructed from the administrative activation procedure and, where that field is blank, from the founding decrees of the measures concerned. Contents: the analytical dataset (31 variables); a codebook; a procedure coding table with the normative source of every coding decision; a crosswalk matching 39 measures to the official monitoring of the statutory 40 per cent Southern allocation obligation; municipality-level residuals from the implementation models; global Moran's I under three alternative spatial weight matrices; local Moran statistics on the downstream residual; the reported model results; the extraction script; and a replication script that reproduces the dataset and every estimate from the raw inputs. WHY THIS PACKAGE IS NECESSARY. The primary source is neither versioned nor stable. While this dataset was being constructed, the same endpoint returned 280,767 records dated 26 February 2026 and, hours later, 291,387 records dated 13 June 2026, while the published CSV files carried 298,338 records; between those two responses the numeric identifiers of both projects and implementing organisations were reassigned. A replication attempt that re-downloaded from source would not reproduce these figures, and no version parameter is available to request a specific extraction. The archived snapshot in this package is the only reproducible reference. TWO TRAPS THAT FAIL SILENTLY. ISTAT codes and fiscal codes lose leading zeros if read as numeric, producing empty joins with no error; in the source organisation register, fiscal codes are stored inconsistently with and without leading zeros, and normalising to eleven digits reduces 13,126 records labelled as municipalities to 7,902 distinct entities. Numeric project identifiers are not stable join keys, coinciding across extractions in only 52.9 per cent of cases; the CUP is not unique. Use the local project code. SPATIAL ANALYSIS. Municipal geometries are the official Istat boundaries at 1 January 2021, joined on the six-digit code. The boundary file is not redistributed here and should be obtained from Istat. Three weight matrices are reported — queen contiguity, eight nearest neighbours and a fifty-kilometre distance band — because they are not interchangeable on subsamples: queen contiguity strands as isolates not only islands but mainland municipalities whose neighbours do not belong to the subsample, and those units are dropped silently from the statistic. Isolate counts are reported for every specification. The duration residual was the pre-specified primary diagnostic and the downstream residual was examined subsequently; both are reported in that order. The package contains no personal data: all implementing bodies are public administrations.
title: Allocation regimes and the territorial conversion of recovery funds: replication package for 71,548 municipal projects under Italy's National Recovery and Resilience Plan

ISTAT codes and fiscal codes lose leading zeros if read as numeric, producing empty joins with no error; in the source organisation register, fiscal codes are stored inconsistently with and without leading zeros, and normalising to eleven digits reduces 13,126 records labelled as municipalities to 7,902 distinct entities. Numeric project identifiers are not stable join keys, coinciding across extractions in only 52.9 per cent of cases; the CUP is not unique. Use the local project code. SPATIAL ANALYSIS. Municipal geometries are the official Istat boundaries at 1 January 2021, joined on the six-digit code. The boundary file is not redistributed here and should be obtained from Istat. Three weight matrices are reported — queen contiguity, eight nearest neighbours and a fifty-kilometre distance band — because they are not interchangeable on subsamples: queen contiguity strands as isolates not only islands but mainland municipalities whose neighbours do not belong to the subsample, and those units are dropped silently from the statistic. Isolate counts are reported for every specification. The duration residual was the pre-specified primary diagnostic and the downstream residual was examined subsequently; both are reported in that order. The package contains no personal data: all implementing bodies are public administrations.
title: Allocation regimes and the territorial conversion of recovery funds: replication package for 71,548 municipal projects under Italy's National Recovery and Resilience Plan

summary: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.
title: SlideRule

summary: L'Ange des projections lumineuses was a monthly journal published for the Œuvre des projections catéchistiques of Champtercier (Basses-Alpes), printed at Lyon, and edited by the abbé Georges Aillaud. It ran from 15 October 1902 to 15 September 1903 as the organ of a subscription lending library that circulated magic-lantern slide sets to village clergy, together with the technical advice, lecture texts and equipment notices needed to use them. This deposit is a complete transcription of the ten issues held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France — 198 pages. Numbers 10 and 11, July and August 1903, are absent from the BnF holdings and no copies have been located elsewhere. The journal documents a working provincial distribution network at the moment cinema was arriving in rural France: it lists the slide sets in circulation and their prices, reports what was shown and where, argues over illuminants and apparatus, and by its final number is advertising a cinematograph alongside the lantern equipment. Its technical columns are a detailed record of alcohol, Auer and acetylene illumination in non-commercial exhibition. Method. The text was read from the BnF's page images by a vision language model working on overlapping half-page tiles, without optical character recognition, and then compared word by word by machine against the BnF's own OCR text layer wherever one exists. 1,864 disagreements were found across the 150 pages with a text layer, classified automatically, and checked selectively — not exhaustively — against the page images; eight readings were corrected as a result, and a separate audit for digital artefacts produced a further fifty. Every correction is logged with its evidence. This is machine transcription with editorial checking: it has not been proofread cover to cover against the original and should not be described as though it had. The February, March and April 1903 issues have no BnF text layer, rest on a single reading, and are identified as such. Spelling, accentuation, capitalisation and punctuation follow the page, including where the printing is inconsistent with itself. Contents of this deposit. The reading edition as PDF (119 pp.) and as plain UTF-8 text, both carrying the editorial note as front matter; the per-page source files, which preserve the printed line breaks and their end-of-line hyphens, with the flags raised on each page and a separate folder for the eighteen non-journal leaves; the editorial note; an apparatus of 137 unresolved or adjudicated readings; the full correction log; and the complete uncurated production log, labelled as provenance documentation rather than an apparatus. See README.md. Source. Bibliothèque nationale de France, shelfmark D-72088 (BIS); ISSN 2273-6220; BnF catalogue record cb326930724. Page images: Source gallica.bnf.fr / Bibliothèque nationale de France . Rights. The journal text is in the public domain. The editorial note, annotations, arrangement and other original editorial contributions are licensed under CC BY 4.0 . No copyright is asserted over the underlying public-domain text. Related. A prose introduction to the journal — its publisher, the slide network it served, and its bearing on the arrival of cinema in provincial France — was published at the time of this deposit at billlefurgy.com/ange-des-projections-lumineuses . It is not part of this deposit and is not covered by the method statement above.
title: L'Ange des projections lumineuses: Transcription of the Ten Issues Held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France, 1902–1903

summary: Per-pixel  active-flame  image–mask chips from  Sentinel-2  covering  25 large California wildfires  (acquisitions spanning 2020–2026). The deposit contains  2,148  co-registered pairs of false-colour composites and segmentation masks. Each chip is  512 × 512 pixels at 20 m  (~10.24 km across), rendered as a fixed-stretch RGB composite ( R = B12 / SWIR2 ,  G = B11 / SWIR1 ,  B = B8A / NIR ) so flaming combustion is separable from cloud, smoke, fresh char, and bright reflective surfaces. Masks were generated automatically with a  modified HOTMAP SWIR hotspot rule  (confirmed flame where B12 and B12/B8A exceed conservative thresholds, plus a connected growth tier for cooler front margins). Pixel values are  0 = background ,  1 = active fire , and  255 = no-data  (outside the acquisition footprint). The corpus uses a  leak-free fire holdout : whole incidents are assigned to partitions ( 18 train / 3 validation / 4 test ), so evaluation measures transfer to unseen fires rather than random chips from the same landscape. This archive includes: images/  and  masks/  (2,148 PNG files each) summary.csv  (chip-level metadata) partitions.csv  (fire → split assignment) analyst_review/hand_masks/  ( 233  independently reviewed test chips;  54%  of the test split), for quantifying weak-label agreement at chip/cluster level Companion  code , labelling protocol, baseline training scripts, and manuscript figures are available at:   https://github.com/MohammadrezaNarimaniUCDavis/California_Sentinel2_Active_Fire_Dataset This dataset supports a data article prepared for submission to  Data in Brief (Elsevier).
title: California Sentinel-2 Active-Fire Segmentation Dataset

summary: CHAPTER 15 --- Recension- CDJ Opinion 2026‑27 on Judicial Impartiality and Private Affiliations --- The Collège de déontologie des magistrats de l’ordre judiciaire (CDJ) issued Opinion 2026‑27 on 9 June 2026, clarifying when a judge’s membership in an irregular fraternity (and, by extension, other private associations) is compatible with judicial ethics.   The opinion does not impose an absolute ban, but it establishes a principled, appearance‑based test that elevates objective impartiality and procedural safeguards over formal neutrality toward associative life. --- Context and legal background --- The opinion sits within a broader jurisprudential movement that treats impartiality—especially its objective dimension—as a cardinal requirement of a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR).   European and domestic case law increasingly hold that disqualification may be required where circumstances would give a reasonable, fully informed observer legitimate doubts about a judge’s neutrality, even absent proof of actual bias.  The CDJ’s reasoning mirrors this “appearance of impropriety” standard: what matters is whether the private commitment can plausibly be seen as creating a priority allegiance or solidarity that conflicts with the judicial duty of independence and neutrality. ---  Core holding: conditional incompatibility --- The CDJ frames its answer in two branches: - Incompatibility: Membership is incompatible with judicial deontological obligations when the Masonic oath induces a “prior allegiance or solidarity” that could override judicial duties. - Compatibility with reservations: Where no such prior allegiance is established, membership remains possible but is surrounded by “important reservations” and requires heightened vigilance to ensure independence, impartiality, and neutrality in both fact and appearance. The opinion explicitly links this risk to three structural features often associated with Masonic practice: an oath of allegiance, an obligation of secrecy, and inter‑member solidarity—each of which can undermine public confidence in the judge’s neutrality. ---  The invisibility problem and informational asymmetry --- A distinctive contribution of the opinion is its focus on invisibility. Unlike family ties, professional networks, or financial interests, Masonic membership is typically not verifiable by litigants.  This informational asymmetry prevents parties from invoking standard procedural safeguards (e.g., recusal motions grounded in disclosed relationships), thereby magnifying the appearance risk.   The CDJ effectively treats non‑disclosable affiliations that entail strong internal loyalties as structurally suspect, because they remove the very mechanism—transparency—that allows objective impartiality to be tested and preserved. --- Constitutional and convention tensions --- While the opinion builds on existing case law, it surfaces unresolved tensions with fundamental rights: - Freedom of association and conscience: Judges retain associative rights, and any limitation must be proportionate and necessary in a democratic society.  - Proportionality and legal certainty: Because the CDJ’s opinions are not binding law and cannot by themselves create statutory incompatibilities, the practical force of the guidance relies on its authority and on how disciplinary bodies and courts receive it. These tensions suggest that a future constitutional or convention‑based challenge could refine the balance between associative freedom and the functional requirements of judicial office. ---- Practical implications for judges --- In the interim, judges face a delicate choice: - Seek prior guidance: Given the opinion’s authority, prudent practice is to consult the CDJ (or equivalent ethics bodies) before joining any association whos
title: Chapter 15 - On Judicial Impartiality and Private Affiliations

summary: 2.2.0 A minor version, not a patch: the change below alters what a default run leaves on disk. Nothing about your results, final outputs or logs changes, but a default that deletes files users previously got to keep is more than a patch. Changed Intermediate pfiles are now deleted as the run progresses, at defaults. Each QC step reads a genotype file and writes a new one — callrate reads your input and writes …_callrate , sex reads that and writes …_sex , and so on — so a ten-step run creates ten copies of your data. At GP2 release scale each copy is tens of GiB. Cleanup used to be skipped whenever warn_only was set, and warn-and-continue is the default , so at defaults every copy survived for the whole run. The only way to reclaim the disk was --no-warn , which also turns warn-and-continue into fail-fast — so you could not have both. That is a bad trade on a long run, where warn-and-continue exists precisely so an eight-hour job does not die on one recoverable step. The two flags no longer interfere: | | before | now | |---|---|---| | (default) | keeps every copy | deletes each copy once the next is written | | --full-output | keeps every copy | keeps every copy | | --no-warn | deletes + fail-fast | fail-fast only | | --no-warn --full-output | keeps + fail-fast | keeps + fail-fast | --full-output is now the only switch governing retention; --no-warn is purely failure policy. Peak disk during a run drops from roughly one working copy per step to one overall — on the round-19 full-GP2 run, ~98 GiB written against a ~50 GiB peak. If you relied on the old default to inspect intermediates, pass --full-output — it reproduces the previous behavior exactly. A failed step's input is still kept either way, so a broken run can still be examined.
title: GenoTools

Changed Intermediate pfiles are now deleted as the run progresses, at defaults. Each QC step reads a genotype file and writes a new one — callrate reads your input and writes …_callrate , sex reads that and writes …_sex , and so on — so a ten-step run creates ten copies of your data. At GP2 release scale each copy is tens of GiB. Cleanup used to be skipped whenever warn_only was set, and warn-and-continue is the default , so at defaults every copy survived for the whole run. The only way to reclaim the disk was --no-warn , which also turns warn-and-continue into fail-fast — so you could not have both. That is a bad trade on a long run, where warn-and-continue exists precisely so an eight-hour job does not die on one recoverable step. The two flags no longer interfere: | | before | now | |---|---|---| | (default) | keeps every copy | deletes each copy once the next is written | | --full-output | keeps every copy | keeps every copy | | --no-warn | deletes + fail-fast | fail-fast only | | --no-warn --full-output | keeps + fail-fast | keeps + fail-fast | --full-output is now the only switch governing retention; --no-warn is purely failure policy. Peak disk during a run drops from roughly one working copy per step to one overall — on the round-19 full-GP2 run, ~98 GiB written against a ~50 GiB peak. If you relied on the old default to inspect intermediates, pass --full-output — it reproduces the previous behavior exactly. A failed step's input is still kept either way, so a broken run can still be examined.

summary: The Earth That Heard is not presented as a literary reconstruction built around biblical verses. It records a textual architecture that the author argues is already present in the Torah itself — a structure that emerged through fifteen years of research into Biblical Hebrew morphology, roots, recurring letter patterns, and the internal organization of the text. The essay traces a continuous thread from the murder of Abel in Genesis to Joshua’s altar on Mount Ebal. Motifs that initially appear independent — earth and blood, firstfruit and firstborn, field and El Shaddai, rising and place, sacrifice, Shechem, the opening of the earth, and the return of the firstfruits — progressively converge into a single narrative structure. The central proposal is that Abel’s unfinished offering, Cain’s failure, and the wounded earth are not abandoned episodes: their resolution unfolds across the Torah and reaches completion in Joshua. The work explicitly separates three epistemic levels: Text — what the biblical text states; Reading — what emerges when distant passages are compared; and Implication — the larger interpretation suggested by the resulting structure. The pattern is also tested quantitatively. The present essay contains 136 key verses; the original connection-density test was performed on a pre-set group of 124 verses selected by the narrative. Using the Control Alphabet / Mandatory Root morphology developed in The Road and the Place , the observed network produced Z = 19.37 (p < 0.0002) against 5,000 random permutations. A second, deliberately simpler test removes the seven control letters א, מ, ת, נ, י, ה, ו from every word and performs direct string matching with no root database; it still yields Z = 10.29 (p < 0.0002) , with the same major long-range connections rising to the top. A raw-word test remains significant at Z = 5.17 (p = 0.0013) . A separate anthology comparison tests whether similarly chosen biblical themes automatically generate the same effect. The Ebal/Shechem axis reaches Z = 17.35 , compared with Covenant Z = 10.07 , Jerusalem/Temple Z = 1.60 , Joseph Z = −8.13 , and Tabernacle Z = −7.16 . The result does not statistically prove the theological interpretation; it shows that the textual concentration being interpreted is itself measurable and unusual. A scientific appendix further examines comparative anatomical and genomic parallels associated with one of the essay’s most unexpected motifs, while explicitly distinguishing scientific observation from midrashic interpretation. After fifteen years of work, the author does not regard this as a story invented to fit the text, but as part of a larger architecture that the text itself gradually disclosed — a structure he considers himself fortunate to have uncovered, even if only in part, and to place on record now. Bilingual publication: Hebrew original and English edition.

summary: Automated risk decisions increasingly depend on probabilistic assessments transmitted across organisational and computational boundaries. A probability estimate may remain numerically intact while losing the contextual information required to evaluate its evidentiary dependence — a condition we term Provenance Loss . We introduce Orphaned Inference — a probabilistic output P ( H | E ) that propagates downstream after its contextual qualification is stripped at a transmission boundary — and show that when downstream agents continue scalar-posterior updating using marginal likelihood ratios, the resulting propagation is equivalent to a Na ̈ıve-Bayes-style independence approximation over the correlated evidence sequence. This double-counts the shared environmental signal, producing Directional Context Amplification , quantified by the Cumulative Provenance Amplification (CPA n ) metric. Under environmental context drift ( C 0 → C 1 ), accumulated phantom certainty persists into the post-shift regime as Post-Shift Epistemic Persistence , driving the mean absolute posterior error close to 1 in true-negative states ( H = 0) during the pre-shift period. In risk-analysis terms, provenance loss separates the numerical value of a risk estimate from the evidentiary conditions under which it remains decision-valid: downstream decision makers may receive an apparently precise probability whose effective evidentiary weight is substantially overstated. A Monte Carlo simulation ( N = 5 , 000 trials, n = 15 agent chain) demonstrates the predicted cascade under the specified parameter regime and documents monotone growth of CPA n across sampled correlation values ρ ∈ { 0 , . . . , 0 . 8 } . We propose three provenance-aware risk-control safeguards and discuss their governance trade-offs.
title: Orphaned Inferences in Automated Risk Hierarchies: Na ̈ıve Bayes Amplification under Provenance Loss

summary: Automated risk decisions increasingly depend on probabilistic assessments transmitted across organisational and computational boundaries. A probability estimate may remain numerically intact while losing the contextual information required to evaluate its evidentiary dependence — a condition we term Provenance Loss . We introduce Orphaned Inference — a probabilistic output P ( H | E ) that propagates downstream after its contextual qualification is stripped at a transmission boundary — and show that when downstream agents continue scalar-posterior updating using marginal likelihood ratios, the resulting propagation is equivalent to a Na ̈ıve-Bayes-style independence approximation over the correlated evidence sequence. This double-counts the shared environmental signal, producing Directional Context Amplification , quantified by the Cumulative Provenance Amplification (CPA n ) metric. Under environmental context drift ( C 0 → C 1 ), accumulated phantom certainty persists into the post-shift regime as Post-Shift Epistemic Persistence , driving the mean absolute posterior error close to 1 in true-negative states ( H = 0) during the pre-shift period. summary: This repository contains two LC–MS/MS raw data files (and .mgf versions if needed), associated search parameters, and curated FASTA databases generated from purified fibrinogen clots crosslinked by endogenous FXIIIa or recombinant transglutaminase 2 (TG2). These samples represent a controlled benchmark system for evaluating crosslink-mass spectrometry (XL-MS) software performance on non-cleavable enzymatic Q–K isopeptide bonds. Unlike conventional chemical crosslinkers, these transglutaminase-mediated crosslinks are zero-length modifications formed by ammonia (NH₃) loss, creating unique challenges for false discovery control and site assignment. The datasets are provided to enable transparent, community-driven comparison of XL search engines and to advance methodological development in enzymatic crosslink identification.
title: Open Benchmark Dataset for Enzymatic Q–K Crosslink Identification by LC–MS/MS

summary: A hydro cascade system benchmark for comparing short-term scheduling methods Frontier Falls is an eight-reservoir hydropower cascade with hourly hydrologic and electricity-market forcing, packaged as a fully specified benchmark problem. Its structure is inspired by the Cumberland River reservoir system, but all names, parameters, and operating assumptions have been modified for benchmark use —  nothing in this dataset represents actual reservoir operations, and all inflows are synthetic . Prices are public market data published by ISO New England (see  License ). The benchmark supports hydropower day-ahead scheduling studies with common physical system and shared forcing scenarios. Use cases include: Scheduling optimization  — comparing algorithms (MPC, SDDP, MILP, heuristics) on an identical, reproducible problem. Model coupling  — workflows that couple river-operations models with power-dispatch optimization. AI-agent operations  — LLM agents making bidding and release decisions with tool support. Total installed capacity: 853 MW across four storage projects and four mainstem run-of-river-style projects in a multi-river network. Detailed cascade system specifications are accompanied by five hydrologic scenarios (with 31-member ensemble 168-hour reforecasts) and five market scenarios that include day-ahead real-time (DA-RT) prices and associated reforecasts. direction_title: KUSTO marine data / towfish / sonar provenance [COUNTEREVIDENCE]
summary: Underwater acoustic target recognition has converged on closed-set classification by vessel type, a task that does not answer whether a monitoring system has heard this hull before. We formalise open-set, cross-passage vessel re-identification on public hydrophone data and specify a protocol that removes the two easiest routes to a high score: hull-disjoint splits keyed to MMSI/IMO, galleries and queries from disjoint passages of each hull, source-pure galleries, and an audio-adjudicated transit-deduplication gate. We describe SKANN, a raw-waveform encoder whose front end is a four-scale bank of learned filters fused by selective-kernel attention, trained with an angular-margin objective and an augmentation regime that perturbs recording chain, ambient noise and multipath while preserving the narrowband lines that carry identity. On a 40-hull IARA gallery (96 queries, 98 passage candidates), cross-passage rank-1 is 0.25 for the embedding and 0.26 for an automated narrowband-tonal comparator; the two are statistically indistinguishable at the top of the ranking, the embedding orders the rest of the list more reliably (AUC 0.82 vs 0.76), and their score fusion reaches rank-1 0.35 -- the only contrast that attains nominal significance, presented as evidence of partial complementarity, not as a recommendation. Transit deduplication alone removes a 16-21 point apparent rank-1 advantage, larger than any between-method difference. Two further findings delimit what public data can support: ShipsEar cannot separate hull identity from recording channel under an identity protocol, and cross-network fine-tuning helps vessels seen during fine-tuning but is a null result on unseen ones. The results support analyst triage over a ranked shortlist, not identification. Checkpoint, validation embeddings, transit map and per-query outputs are released under CC-BY-4.0 (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22160138).
title: Open-Set Vessel Re-Identification from Underwater Ship-Radiated Noise with a Raw-Waveform Selective-Kernel Acoustic Neural Network (SKANN) and a Cross-Passage Evaluation Protocol

summary: Predicting underwater acoustic transmission loss rapidly and accurately is crucial for real-time ocean acoustic applications. While Fourier Neural Operators (FNO) have emerged as powerful surrogate models due to their global receptive fields, they suffer from spectral bias. The frequency truncation mechanism in FNO filters out high-frequency components, resulting in over-smoothed predictions that fail to capture fine-grained interference patterns. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes a Spectral-Spatial Residual Learning (S2RL) framework. S2RL decomposes the prediction task into a coarse-to-fine process: a spectral Global Propagator first generates a globally consistent prediction, and a spatial Local Refiner subsequently recovers the high-frequency residuals. Experimental results on a South China Sea dataset show that the proposed method significantly outperforms FNO baselines while maintaining millisecond-level inference speeds.
title: Mitigating Spectral Bias in Neural Operators for Underwater Transmission Loss Prediction

summary: In underwater covert cooperative missions, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) often cannot rely on active sonar to continuously obtain complete information, since active sensing and frequent communications increase the risk of exposure. As a result, AUVs primarily rely on passive observation, an approach that yields incomplete local perception and limited task efficiency. Although underwater acoustic communications can mitigate this limitation through information sharing, they are simultaneously constrained by long delays, severe interference, low reliability, and the risk of covert exposure. Existing communications-oriented multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) studies often model communication as an ideal information flow, whereas traditional communication optimization primarily focuses on link-level performance. However, both are insufficient to characterize the actual contribution of perceptual information to cooperative tasks under realistic conditions of covert physical communications. This paper proposes a Sensed Information Value Realization Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (SVR-MARL) framework that leverages practical information to characterize the utility of information for cooperative tasks and learns distributed cooperative policies under realistic communication and covert constraints. Through a case study of covert multi-AUV cooperative localization and tracking, the potential of the proposed framework to improve collaborative task efficiency while reducing unnecessary communication and exposure risks is demonstrated.
title: Task-Oriented Sensing and Covert Transmissions for Collaborative Multi-AUV Systems
