summary: Model upgrades are routine; memory migrations are not. An agent can keep the same memory store and still forget: a new model may interpret old notes differently, mixed embedding versions may break retrieval, and repair may fail without the original evidence. We compare memory as the same history is preserved verbatim for long-context reading (LC-RAW), divided into chunks for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), compressed by a model into natural-language notes (NOTES), or normalized into a fixed-schema knowledge graph (KG-fixed). The study uses 48 synthetic histories with randomized answer codes, exact scoring, and two open-weight models with sub 10 billion parameters. Our measurements show that fixed-schema structures transfer reliably, with KG-fixed accuracy changing by only $+0.0004 \pm 0.0020$ following a writer swap. Conversely, compressed NOTES exhibit high model coupling, with accuracy shifting asymmetrically by $+9.91$ or $-13.28$ percentage points depending on the specific migration direction. In RAG systems, partial embedding migrations using a 50/50 mixed index capture only a 4.96-point accuracy improvement, forfeiting the majority of the 11.90-point gain achieved through full re-embedding. Diagnostic decomposition attributes 80% ($0.467 \pm 0.014$) of the NOTES accuracy deficit to information lost during initial construction, whereas retrieval failures drive 81% ($0.364 \pm 0.012$) of the RAG deficit. Finally, store-only repair of NOTES fails to reach a 90% performance recovery target in all 48 test cases, whereas retaining the raw source history enables successful recovery in 34 of 48 cases for one tested direction. These findings highlight the necessity of direction-specific migration testing, strict embedding space isolation, and the retention of source histories for memory repair.

summary: Benchmark contamination, where evaluation examples appear in a model's training data, threatens the validity of LLM assessment. Statistical tools for detecting training-data membership exist, but have been validated almost exclusively in controlled academic regimes: large, homogeneous pre-training corpora and transparent, single-stage training pipelines. Whether these methods remain reliable in realistic auditing scenarios remains unclear. We identify two under-studied failure modes: distribution shift, which arises when suspect and validation sets violate the IID assumption, and scale constraints, which arise because benchmarks are orders of magnitude smaller than pre-training corpora. We systematically evaluate three leading paradigms, LLM Dataset Inference, Post-Hoc Dataset Inference, and CoDeC, across 25 models from multiple families (including Pythia, OLMo 2, and specialised cultural and medical LLMs) and scales (up to 27B). We then further extend our analysis to frontier industry models. Across 335 evaluations, only 201 yield correct outcomes. LLM Dataset Inference results in false positives under distribution shift, Post-Hoc Dataset Inference is underpowered at benchmark scale, and CoDeC provides only coarse provenance signals that are insufficient to verify individual benchmark splits. Our results reveal a systematic reliability gap between controlled validation and practical benchmark auditing, and show that statistical detection cannot yet replace transparent data provenance. summary: European digital sovereignty and security increasingly depend on whether high-impact decisions can be grounded in location evidence that remains credible under adversarial pressure. This paper frames a cross-sector analysis as a location-data provenance problem: whether there is contestable evidence about where and when an asserted event occurred, who or what produced the assertion, what a device or service reported as location, and which audit and retention guarantees apply. summary: Provenance plays a crucial role in scientific workflow execution, for instance by providing data for failure analysis, real-time monitoring, or statistics on resource utilization for right-sizing allocations. The workflows themselves, however, become increasingly complex in terms of involved components. Furthermore, they are executed on distributed cluster infrastructures, which makes the real-time collection, integration, and analysis of provenance data challenging. Existing provenance systems struggle to balance scalability, real-time processing, online provenance analytics, and integration across different components and compute resources. Moreover, most provenance solutions are not workflow-aware; by focusing on arbitrary workloads, they miss opportunities for workflow systems where optimization and analysis can exploit the availability of a workflow specification that dictates, to some degree, task execution orders and provides abstractions for physical tasks at a logical level. In this paper, we present HyProv, a hybrid provenance management system that combines centralized and federated paradigms to offer scalable, online, and workflow-aware queries over workflow provenance traces. HyProv uses a centralized component for efficient management of the small and stable workflow-specification-specific provenance, and complements this with federated querying over different scalable monitoring and provenance databases for the large-scale execution logs. This enables low-latency access to current execution data. Furthermore, the design supports complex provenance queries, which we exemplify for the workflow system Airflow in combination with the resource manager Kubernetes. Our experiments indicate that HyProv scales to large workflows, answers provenance queries with sub-second latencies, and adds only modest CPU and memory overhead to the cluster.
title: HyProv: Hybrid Provenance Management for Scientific Workflows

summary: In modern engineering practice, human engineers collaborate in specialized teams to design complex products, with each expert completing their respective tasks while communicating and exchanging results and data with one another. While this division of expertise is essential for managing multidisciplinary complexity, it demands substantial development time and cost. Recently, we introduced OpenFOAMGPT (1.0, 2.0), which functions as an autonomous AI engineer for computational fluid dynamics, and turbulence.ai, which can conduct end-to-end research in fluid mechanics draft publications and PhD theses. Building upon these foundations, we present Engineering.ai, a platform for teams of AI engineers in computational design. The framework employs a hierarchical multi-agent architecture where a Chief Engineer coordinates specialized agents consisting of Aerodynamics, Structural, Acoustic, and Optimization Engineers, each powered by LLM with domain-specific knowledge. Agent-agent collaboration is achieved through file-mediated communication for data provenance and reproducibility, while a comprehensive memory system maintains project context, execution history, and retrieval-augmented domain knowledge to ensure reliable decision-making across the workflow. The system integrates FreeCAD, Gmsh, OpenFOAM, CalculiX, and BPM acoustic analysis, enabling parallel multidisciplinary simulations while maintaining computational accuracy. The framework is validated through UAV wing optimization. This work demonstrates that agentic-AI-enabled AI engineers has the potential to perform complex engineering tasks autonomously. Remarkably, the automated workflow achieved a 100% success rate across over 400 parametric configurations, with zero mesh generation failures, solver convergence issues, or manual interventions required, validating that the framework is trustworthy.
title: Engineering.ai: A Platform for Teams of AI Engineers in Computational Design

summary: AI deployment increasingly resembles a pipeline of data transformation, fine-tuning, and agent interactions rather than a monolithic LLM job; recent examples include RLHF/RLAIF training and agentic workflows. To cope with this shift, we propose FlowMesh, a multi-tenant service fabric that executes and optimizes these workloads as one shared service instead of isolated pipelines. It decomposes workflows into fine-grained operators with recorded lineage, enabling de-duplication of work across users and batching requests on the same hardware while preserving per-workflow provenance. A global control plane maintains a cluster-wide pool of ready operators and uses a single utility function to pick both the batch and the worker, balancing throughput, cost, and data locality on heterogeneous GPUs. The data plane is an elastic fleet of stateless workers backed by a content-addressable store, enabling rapid, automatic scale-out, safe retry after preemption, and portability across managed clusters such as Kubernetes and geo-distributed GPU marketplaces such as Vast.ai. Compared with baseline solutions, FlowMesh achieves up to 3.8x cost reduction and 2.0x lower energy usage, provides a similar or better latency profile, and remains efficient under dynamic and failure-prone conditions.
title: FlowMesh: A Service Fabric for Composable LLM Workflows

summary: Autonomous Vehicles (AV) proliferation brings important and pressing security and reliability issues that must be dealt with to guarantee public safety and help their widespread adoption. The contribution of the proposed research is towards achieving more secure, reliable, and trustworthy autonomous transportation system by providing more capabilities for anomaly detection, data provenance, and real-time response in safety critical AV deployments. In this research, we develop a new framework that combines the power of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for real-time anomaly detection with blockchain technology to detect and prevent any malicious activity including sensor failures in AVs. Through Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, our approach continually monitors associated multi-sensor data streams to detect anomalous patterns that may represent cyberattacks as well as hardware malfunctions. Further, this framework employs a decentralized platform for securely storing sensor data and anomaly alerts in a blockchain ledger for data incorruptibility and authenticity, while offering transparent forensic features. Moreover, immediate automated response mechanisms are deployed using smart contracts when anomalies are found. This makes the AV system more resilient to attacks from both cyberspace and hardware component failure. Besides, we identify potential challenges of scalability in handling high frequency sensor data, computational constraint in resource constrained environment, and of distributed data storage in terms of privacy.
title: AI-Powered Anomaly Detection with Blockchain for Real-Time Security and Reliability in Autonomous Vehicles

summary: A provenance analysis for a query evaluation or a model checking computation extracts information on how its result depends on the atomic facts of the model or database. Traditional work on data provenance was, to a large extent, restricted to positive query languages or the negation-free fragment of first-order logic and showed how provenance abstractions can be usefully described as elements of commutative semirings -- most generally as multivariate polynomials with positive integer coefficients. We describe and evaluate here a provenance approach for dealing with negation, based on quotient semirings of polynomials with dual indeterminates. This not only provides a semiring provenance analysis for full first-order logic (and other logics and query languages with negation) but also permits a reverse provenance analysis, i.e., finding models that satisfy various properties under given provenance tracking assumptions. We describe the potential for applications to explaining missing query answers or failures of integrity constraints, and to using these explanations for computing repairs. This approach also is the basis of a systematic study of semiring semantics in a broad logical context.
title: Provenance Analysis and Semiring Semantics for First-Order Logic

summary: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for complex decision-making in autonomous systems and air combat. While MARL has demonstrated significant potential in air combat, achieving sophisticated tactical coordination remains a non-trivial challenge. This difficulty is largely attributed to two primary limitations: (1) the absence of structured relational modeling hinders agents from capturing complex, time-varying interactions among battlefield entities; and (2) conventional flat architectures often lack the capability to explicitly model tactical roles, leading to ambiguous task allocation in highly dynamic environments. To address these challenges, we propose Hierarchical Dynamic Role-Graph Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (DRG-MAPPO), a novel MARL framework that integrates graph-based relational modeling with dynamic role assignment. Specifically, DRG-MAPPO constructs a graph-based representation of battlefield interactions and leverages graph attention mechanisms to extract critical relational features among allies, enemies, and threats. Subsequently, a high-level policy employs a dynamic role assignment mechanism to determine tactical responsibilities (e.g., ``leader'' and ``supporter''). Conditioned on these roles and encoded graph-relational features, a low-level policy executes discrete maneuver actions, facilitating the joint optimization of tactical strategy and collaborative execution. Furthermore, a target-priority auxiliary task is designed to foster the emergence of behaviors such as focus-fire. Experimental results demonstrate that DRG-MAPPO achieves a state-of-the-art win rate of 87%, suggesting that our framework effectively balances relational modeling, interpretability, and optimization stability for cooperative air combat.
title: DRG-MAPPO: Hierarchical Dynamic Role-Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Air Combat

summary: The coordination of Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) in high-density industrial environments represents a critical challenge within Logistics 4.0, as traditional traffic management methods often lead to inefficiencies caused by negotiation-based priority assignment. To overcome the resulting limitations, this paper presents an innovative AGV traffic management system based on a Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding (L-MAPF) algorithm operating on roadmaps generated with Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS) curves. The approach guarantees locally optimal coordination and ensures safe operation of large and heterogeneous AGVs. Building on this concept, the proposed framework integrates a modified version of the Bounded Horizon Conflict Based Search (CBS) technique within a Rolling Horizon Conflict Resolution strategy, utilizing an extended time horizon for each agent to enable effective conflict resolution in corridors identified by a topological map. In contrast to state-of-the-art methods for AGV fleet traffic management, the proposed solution is designed for real-world, non-standardized (i.e., non-grid-like) industrial settings characterized by narrow bidirectional corridors and high-traffic density, where AGVs of various sizes and capabilities operate simultaneously. Key contributions include an anytime conflict resolution strategy with adaptive time horizon regulation, an execution layer for safe and standard-compliant interaction with real AGVs, and an advanced mechanism for deadlock detection and resolution. Experimental results obtained in realistic industrial environments demonstrate higher throughput, with improvements of up to 11% over a conventional rule-based traffic management system, a state-of-the-art industrial method, and a priority-based L-MAPF variant, while maintaining continuous operation and improved efficiency.
title: A traffic management system for large and heterogeneous vehicles in narrow industrial environments

summary: Calibration release: the package's no-shipped-coefficients policy finally comes with the tool that closes the loop. Every shipped set carries the caveat that lever arms depend on material, mode pair, excitation and substrate; calibrate_lever_arms turns reference measurements you control -- a strain-stage sweep, a gated sweep, any points with known (strain, density) -- into your own fitted coefficient matrix, with uncertainties and provenance. New in ramansep.calibration calibrate_lever_arms : weighted least-squares fit of the (m, 2) lever-arm matrix, one linear problem per mode on the shared reference design. With shift sigmas the parameter covariance is the exact known-noise Gauss-Markov result and a per-mode chi-square consistency check comes back with it; without sigmas the covariance uses the residual variance, which is why that path refuses fewer than three reference points instead of inventing an error bar. Identifiability refused, not fudged : reference states collinear in the (strain, density) plane (a strain-only sweep, or gating that strains proportionally) cannot separately determine the two arms of any mode -- the fit raises with an explanation instead of returning one of infinitely many minimizers. CalibrationResult.coefficients() packages a two-mode calibration as a ModeCoefficients with a MANDATORY provenance string; result.K feeds MultiModeModel directly for m > 2. Anchors (asserted in the tests, not stated) Noise-free shifts from a known matrix are recovered to machine precision, with zero estimated uncertainty. The hand-built normal-equation solution agrees with an independent QR solve ( numpy.linalg.lstsq on the whitened system) to 1e-10. The orthogonal unit design {(1,0), (0,1)} with unit sigmas has EXACTLY the identity parameter covariance -- the closed form, not an approximation. Seeded Monte-Carlo scatter of the fitted arms matches the reported sigmas. Degenerate and malformed reference sets raise (collinear designs, n = 1, n = 2 without sigmas, non-positive sigmas, non-finite shifts). The full round trip -- calibrate on synthetic references, package the coefficients, invert forward-generated maps through SeparationModel -- returns the input strain and density maps to 1e-10. 50 tests across Python 3.9-3.13. Install: pip install -U ramansep .
title: ramansep: two-mode separation of strain and carrier density in 2D-material Raman maps

summary: Python package and command-line tool that estimates the share of variance in an antimicrobial resistance phenotype carried by the lineages of a bacterial collection, from a lineage label and a susceptibility call or a recorded dilution, and refuses the estimate where the collection cannot support one. One collection admits three quantities and the package reports them apart: the lineage-membership share, what a rule scored out of sample reaches, with a lineage bootstrap; the design-corrected component ratio of the same collection, with an interval exact under the Gaussian one-way model by inversion of a noncentral F; and the superpopulation share for the species, with a chi-square layer on the number of lineages. Each is scored against its own truth on 135 simulated cells from five lineages to a thousand, and each sits behind a gate that refuses where the collection cannot identify the quantity or the residuals contradict the law the interval assumes, the coverage of each having been measured. summary: PIHR-RH-XXVII reduced the arithmetic obstruction in the Prime Integrator-Holonomy-Recursion (PIHR) programme to a sharply localized centered endpoint-plus-tail functional after exact removal of the divergent harmonic prime spine. The present paper develops the subsequent analysis and records several new exact identities, structural no-go results, and a substantially weaker sufficient arithmetic target. First, a new nonlinear crossing storage is introduced. It is constant between prime-power impulses and telescopes exactly to an exponential expression involving the reciprocal von Mangoldt sum and the critical square-root-weighted von Mangoldt sum. At an interpolated Euler-constant downcrossing the nonlinear storage coincides with the critical tangent. This gives a compact exponential Euler formulation of the crossing problem. Second, a first-contact analysis of the Jordan-Riesz deformation shows that the Laplace moment route does not by itself bypass the critical sign problem: complete monotonicity of the limiting moment function would essentially re-encode positivity of the underlying tangent. An interval version of the Jordan deformation nevertheless removes a different obstruction, namely numerator cancellation at hypothetical off-critical zeta zeros. The subsequent fixed-parameter transfer audit shows why asymptotic Selberg production dominance does not automatically imply positivity of the centered Jordan-Riesz state: after complete subtraction of the elementary finite-Euler modes, the same harmonic 1/p   prime-spine operator reappears independently of the deformation parameter. Third, a direct energy calculation at an exact Euler-constant crossing yields a new identity for the tangent J(T) . The identity separates a positive quadratic history, a positive diagonal contribution, and a single ordered impulse-history correlation. Polarization of that correlation produces an exact nonnegative pair-dispersion energy. Splitting the pair interaction at the multiplicative hyperbola  mn = x   then separates a causal Selberg pair sector from an overdiagonal sector. The causal sector is controlled by genuine positive multiplicative pair production, while the overdiagonal sector becomes an exact complementary-scale deficit difference D(T-t)-D(t) , exhibiting a largest-prime/least-prime duality consistent with the finite-Euler analysis of PIHR-RH-XXVI. Finally, the Landau endpoint is weakened. Exact eventual positivity of J   is stronger than necessary: under the stated transform-continuation hypotheses, a lower bound J(T)>-e o(T)    already excludes every hypothetical zeta zero with real part greater than 1/2. Consequently the remaining arithmetic problem need not orient the centered pair-transport remainder pointwise; it is sufficient to bound its negative part subexponentially. This is a materially weaker target than the crossing inequality itself. The principal remaining problem is an unconditional subexponential one-sided estimate for the centered overdiagonal Selberg pair transport, preserving its multiplicative orientation after the linear prime-spine telescope.
title: Crossing Energy, Ordered Selberg Pair Transport, and a Subexponential Landau Reduction of the Remaining Riemann-Hypothesis Obstruction

summary: Characterization release: the shipped recipes are Jung et al.'s six junctions; yours needs its own (Ic0, Tc*, tau) before any budget in this package applies to it. The standard measurement -- critical current versus temperature -- determines exactly those parameters, and fit_ic_curve implements the fit against the package's own short-junction ensemble. New in absnoise.icfit fit_ic_curve : bounded nonlinear least squares of Ic(T) = Ic0 M(T; Tc, tau)/M(0) with the BCS gap solved from the gap equation (no tanh shortcut). Ic0 absorbs channel count and series factors; Tc sets the gap scale; tau is identified by the SHAPE of the suppression -- transparent junctions keep their supercurrent to higher T/Tc than tunnel junctions. With measurement sigmas: exact known-noise covariance plus a chi-square consistency check. A curve that never leaves the low-temperature plateau triggers a warning that Tc and tau are weakly determined, instead of a well-formatted result implying a well-determined one. IcFit.to_recipe : packages the fit with your measured geometry (xi, L, W, Vbg, Rn -- values an Ic(T) curve does not determine, so the method does not pretend to) as a Recipe , and every thermometry and calorimetry budget in the package applies to your junction directly. ic_model : the forward model exposed on its own, with the closed-form zero-temperature maximizing phase sin^2(phi*/2) = (1 - sqrt(1 - tau))/tau used for normalization. Anchors (asserted in the tests, not stated) The closed-form T = 0 maximizing phase equals a dense phase-grid maximum to 1e-8 across transparencies from 0.05 to 0.99. The fit's forward model agrees with the package's independent ShortJunction.Ic implementation to machine precision on every shipped recipe and temperature tested. Noise-free synthetic curves return the generating (Ic0, Tc, tau) to 1e-5 or better, with chi-square consistent with exact data. Seeded Monte-Carlo scatter of the fitted parameters is compatible with the reported sigmas, and the recovered Tc is unbiased at the tested noise level. Malformed and unconstraining data are refused or warned about (too few points, no sigmas with n = 4, negative currents, non-finite values, plateau-only temperature ranges). A fitted recipe re-enters the pipeline: the calibrated ShortJunction built from it reproduces the input curve to 1e-4. 62 tests across Python 3.9-3.13. Install: pip install -U absnoise .
title: absnoise: Andreev-bound-state occupation noise and detector budgets for proximity Josephson junctions

summary: This dataset accompanies “Population-scale burden analysis of rare damaging coding variants identifies novel risk genes for Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias and Parkinson’s disease and related disorders” by Le Guen, Peña-Tauber and colleagues. The release contains 16 gzip-compressed, tab-delimited gene-based burden summary-statistic files covering Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), and Parkinson’s disease and related disorders (PDRD); combined-proxy and direct-diagnosis ascertainment; and all-ancestry (ALL) and European-ancestry (EUR) analyses. The files share 61 columns and contain 1,000,189 retained gene/mask analysis rows in total, including nonsignificant results. The four nested masks comprise high-confidence loss-of-function variants alone or together with qualifying missense variants at REVEL thresholds of 0.75, 0.50 or 0.25. The associated manuscript specifies GRCh38 coordinates. The primary discovery analyses are AD combined-proxy ALL and PD combined-proxy ALL. EUR analyses are secondary ancestry analyses; AD-direct and PD-direct are secondary, nested phenotype-sensitivity analyses. All ADRD/PDRD analyses are diagnostic-sensitivity comparisons. Combined-proxy includes direct cases and family-history-only proxy cases, not proxy cases alone. Phenotype definitions and ancestry strata overlap and are not independent replication datasets. The release explicitly separates effect estimation from association evidence. REGENIE-only effect estimates combine compatible binary-outcome burden models from UK Biobank, All of Us and ADSP for AD/ADRD, or UK Biobank, All of Us and AMP-PD for PD/PDRD. Combined-proxy cohort effects use the revised exact common-control mixture-model inversion under kappa=0.5. ADES stage-1 estimates from Holstege et al. (2022) are reported separately because their ordinal summed-dosage model differs from the REGENIE binary-outcome maximum-allele burden model. Eligible ADES and REGENIE results are integrated through effective-sample-size-weighted signed-Z evidence; no ADES-inclusive pooled odds ratio is calculated. Use P_OVERALL or LOG10P_OVERALL for final association evidence, and the BETA_REGENIE, SE_REGENIE and REGENIE odds-ratio/confidence-interval columns for the pooled REGENIE effect estimate. AD/ADRD overall evidence falls back to REGENIE when eligible ADES evidence is unavailable. ADES does not contribute to PD/PDRD. The same ADES source is reused across AD-family comparisons and ancestry strata. The README and column dictionary define all fields, missing-value conventions, numerical precision and interpretation. A public manifest and checksums document all 16 files. The dataset contains aggregate gene-level results, not individual-level genotypes or single-variant summary statistics. Dataset DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22702628. License selected for this record: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0).
title: Population-scale burden analysis of rare damaging coding variants identifies novel risk genes for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias and Parkinson's disease and related disorders

summary: Modern large language model research agents, commonly marketed under the label deep research, are highly capable at locating sources, verifying claims, and synthesizing existing literature into structured reports. This capability has not translated into a comparable capacity for scientific discovery. We argue that this gap has a specific, testable cause, which we call literature attracti on: the more strongly a generation process is grounded in retrieved literature, the more its outputs converge toward concepts already dominant in that literature, at the expense of novelty. We separate four quantities that are routinely conflated in evaluations of AI research systems: research depth, research novelty, research validity, and research value. We review the current frontier of deep research systems and automated science pipelines, describe the attention-level mechanisms that plausibly cause literature attraction in retrieval-augmented generation, and propose a controlled experimental protocol to measure the novelty-grounding tradeoff dir ectly, using embedding-based and graph-based novelty metrics, a temporal hold-out benchmark, and human expert validation. We then outline an architectural response: a two-stage exploit-then-explore pipeline in which a quality-diversity search process is used to deliberately push hypothesis generation into regions of the concept space that are underrepresented in the retrieved literature, while an adversarial falsification agent constrains the resulting hypotheses to remain scientificall y testable. We close with a proposed output format, the research novelty report, that reports where a generated hypothesis sits relative to existing knowledge rather than asserting that it is novel. This paper is a research proposal and experimental design; it does not claim to have already demonstrated the phenomenon it sets out to measure.
title: Escaping the Literature: Exploring New Scientific Ideas with Large Language Models

summary: Reliability Beyond Accuracy in Crop Classification Benchmarks (Supplementary Materials) Introduction: Near-perfect crop-label accuracy can conceal uncertainty, perturbation sensitivity, and weak explanations. This study evaluates these reliability dimensions without treating benchmark classification as agronomic recommendation. Materials and Methods: Ten classifiers were evaluated using five matched stratified fitting, validation, and test partitions on a 2,200-record crop-label benchmark and an independent 3,810-record rice-grain benchmark. A Calibrated Selective Forest combined Random Forest, validation-fitted temperature scaling, and confidence-based abstention. Analyses included feature and component ablations, probability calibration, Gaussian input perturbations, computational cost, and explanation fidelity. Results: Mean crop-label accuracy was 99.59% for Random Forest, 99.23% for XGBoost, and 98.32% for FT-Transformer. Random Forest calibration reduced mean expected calibration error from 0.0449 to 0.0038. At a 0.95 threshold, calibrated selection retained 98.59% of predictions with 0.091% mean selective error. Under perturbations of 0.20 training standard deviations, its accuracy fell to 86.96% and selective error rose to 4.29%. On rice grains, Random Forest accuracy was 91.71%, and calibration did not improve every probability metric. Local explanation rankings were often stable despite a median neighborhood weighted R² of 0.293 under the specified local interpretable model-agnostic explanations (LIME) configuration. Conclusions: Accuracy, calibration, selective reliability, and explanation fidelity are distinct properties. The composite pipeline provides an auditable benchmark procedure, not a new learning algorithm or a validated farm recommendation system. Geographic and temporal agronomic validation remain necessary.
title: Reliability Beyond Accuracy in Crop Classification Benchmarks (Supplementary Materials)

summary: This reproducibility package accompanies a measurement-science workflow for temporal light modulation (TLM) metric reproduction and computational sensitivity analysis. summary: Processed data and analysis code supporting “Horizontal wind estimation from consumer-drone hover telemetry: comparing machine-learning and calibration approaches.” The dataset covers 50 DJI Air 3S hover sessions at two sites in Bremen, Germany, with reference wind measurements from a TriSonica Mini ultrasonic anemometer. The study compares Ridge regression with a tilt-based calibration baseline for estimating horizontal wind from drone telemetry. The archive includes aligned 10 Hz data, derived features, calibration measurements, fitted models, held-out predictions, validation metrics, and processing and plotting scripts. Raw flight and anemometer logs are not included but are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

summary: This repository contains supplementary documentation for a qualitative interview study examining how Bachelor of Software Engineering students understand and use generative AI in their studies. The study investigates: (1) the roles students assign to generative AI and how these roles are enacted; (2) how generative AI transforms learning and software-development tasks and how students legitimize its adoption; and (3) how students negotiate and exercise agency when working with generative AI. The package includes: the interview guide and replication material; First Cycle codebooks organized by research question; Second Cycle Pattern Codes and explanations of their analytical development; a code-saturation monitoring record tracing code emergence, elaboration, and confirmation across interviews; and supplementary evidence tables supporting the reported findings. The interviews were analyzed using the two-cycle coding approach described by Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña. First Cycle coding combined descriptive, process, and values-oriented codes. During Second Cycle analysis, conceptually related First Cycle codes were synthesized into broader Pattern Codes. Interview recordings and full transcripts are not publicly available because they contain potentially identifying contextual information and were collected under confidentiality commitments. The package therefore supports analytical transparency and methodological replication without releasing the underlying confidential data. The materials should be interpreted in relation to the educational and institutional context reported in the associated publication. The codebooks and Pattern Codes represent an inductively developed analytical framework rather than a universal taxonomy of student AI adoption.

summary: Replication data and code for an analysis of how allocation procedures shape which Italian municipalities obtain Recovery and Resilience Facility resources, and whether they convert them into completed works. The package covers 68,990 projects implemented by municipal governments across 36 plan measures, extracted from the OpenPNRR REST API at the ReGiS extraction date of 13 June 2026. Each project carries a coded allocation regime — open window, competitive, administrative assignment, or decentralised regional selection — reconstructed from the administrative activation procedure and, where that field is blank, from the founding decrees of the measures concerned. Contents: the analytical dataset (31 variables); a codebook; a procedure coding table with the normative source of every coding decision; a crosswalk matching 39 measures to the official monitoring of the statutory 40 per cent Southern allocation obligation; municipality-level residuals from the implementation models; global Moran's I under three alternative spatial weight matrices; local Moran statistics on the downstream residual; the reported model results; the extraction script; and a replication script that reproduces the dataset and every estimate from the raw inputs. WHY THIS PACKAGE IS NECESSARY. The primary source is neither versioned nor stable. While this dataset was being constructed, the same endpoint returned 280,767 records dated 26 February 2026 and, hours later, 291,387 records dated 13 June 2026, while the published CSV files carried 298,338 records; between those two responses the numeric identifiers of both projects and implementing organisations were reassigned. A replication attempt that re-downloaded from source would not reproduce these figures, and no version parameter is available to request a specific extraction. The archived snapshot in this package is the only reproducible reference. TWO TRAPS THAT FAIL SILENTLY. ISTAT codes and fiscal codes lose leading zeros if read as numeric, producing empty joins with no error; in the source organisation register, fiscal codes are stored inconsistently with and without leading zeros, and normalising to eleven digits reduces 13,126 records labelled as municipalities to 7,902 distinct entities. Numeric project identifiers are not stable join keys, coinciding across extractions in only 52.9 per cent of cases; the CUP is not unique. Use the local project code. SPATIAL ANALYSIS. Municipal geometries are the official Istat boundaries at 1 January 2021, joined on the six-digit code. The boundary file is not redistributed here and should be obtained from Istat. Three weight matrices are reported — queen contiguity, eight nearest neighbours and a fifty-kilometre distance band — because they are not interchangeable on subsamples: queen contiguity strands as isolates not only islands but mainland municipalities whose neighbours do not belong to the subsample, and those units are dropped silently from the statistic. Isolate counts are reported for every specification. The duration residual was the pre-specified primary diagnostic and the downstream residual was examined subsequently; both are reported in that order. The package contains no personal data: all implementing bodies are public administrations.
title: Allocation regimes and the territorial conversion of recovery funds: replication package for 71,548 municipal projects under Italy's National Recovery and Resilience Plan

summary: SlideRule is an open source server-side framework for on-demand processing of science data in the cloud. The SlideRule project offers a new paradigm for NASA archival data management – rapid delivery of customizable on-demand data products, rather than hosting large volumes of standard derivative products, which will inevitably be insufficient for some science applications. The scalable server-side components of SlideRule run in the AWS cloud with optimized functions to read HDF5 data hosted by NASA in S3 cloud object storage. While SlideRule can be accessed by any HTTP client (e.g., curl) through GET and POST requests, the sliderule-python client provides a user-friendly API for synchronous interaction with the SlideRule service. The client library returns standard Python data containers (i.e., Pandas DataFrame) and facilitates serialization with provenance metadata for reproducible science. SlideRule uses a plugin framework to support different NASA missions and data products. The ICESat-2 SlideRule plugin offers customizable algorithms to process the archive of low-level data products from the NASA Ice Cloud and land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) laser altimetry mission. The user defines a geographic area of interest and key processing parameters via an interactive web interface or the API, and SlideRule returns high-level surface elevation point cloud products in seconds to minutes, enabling rapid algorithm development, visualization and scientific interpretation.
title: SlideRule

summary: Background: Surface roughness is an important characteristic of resin composite restorations and may be influenced by material composition and finishing and polishing procedures. Objective: To evaluate changes in surface roughness (Ra) of nanofilled, nanohybrid, and microhybrid resin composites after sequential finishing and polishing and to compare their final surface roughness. Materials and Methods: S ixty disc-shaped specimens (8 mm × 2 mm; shade A2) were fabricated using Filtek Z350 XT, IPS Empress Direct, and Filtek Z250 (n = 20 per material). Fifteen specimens per material underwent a standardized finishing and polishing protocol using fine- and extra-fine-grit diamond burs followed by sequential Sof-Lex discs, while five specimens per material remained untreated as controls. Surface roughness was measured using a Mitutoyo SJ-210 contact profilometer at baseline   and after the intervention. Because specimen-level identification was not preserved between measurement sessions, baseline and final measurements were analyzed as independent observations using independent-samples t-tests, with Welch’s correction when required. Final Ra values among materials were compared using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey HSD tests (α = 0.05). Results: All three experimental composites showed statistically significant increases in Ra after finishing and polishing (all p < 0.001), whereas no statistically significant changes were observed in the untreated controls (all p > 0.05). Mean Ra increased from 0.085 to 0.181 μm for IPS Empress Direct, from 0.111 to 0.186 μm for Filtek Z350 XT, and from 0.122 to 0.195 μm for Filtek Z250. Final Ra values did not differ significantly among the three materials (F(2,42) = 0.559, p = 0.576). Conclusions: Sequential finishing and polishing significantly increased surface roughness relative to the strip-polymerized baseline surfaces of all three resin composites, without statistically significant differences in final Ra among the materials. The final mean Ra values remained below the predefined 0.2 μm surface-roughness threshold. Under the experimental conditions evaluated, post-polishing surface roughness could not be predicted solely on the basis of nanofilled, nanohybrid, or microhybrid filler classification.
title: Surface Roughness of Nanofilled, Nanohybrid, and Microhy-brid Resin Composites After Sequential Finishing and Polish-ing: An In Vitro Comparative Study

summary: This deposit contains the results replication package for the article “Governing the Eurasian Roundabout: Anti-Circumvention Governance and Post-Soviet Intermediaries after 2022.” It reconstructs the article’s quantitative trade evidence from archived Eurostat Easy Comext data and provides structured versions of all numbered tables and figures. The product-specific analysis covers monthly EU27 exports from January 2019 through December 2025 for the 50 six-digit Harmonized System codes in the February 2024 Common High Priority Items list and 13 destinations. The workflow constructs the balanced product–partner–month panel, aggregates partner–month exports, calculates raw and normalized summaries, compares product-specific growth with total-export growth, estimates descriptive partner- and month-fixed-effects paths, and reproduces the reported comparison windows and sensitivity checks. The reconstructed evidence shows a sharp contraction in mean monthly EU exports of Common High Priority Items to Russia, from EUR 295.7 million in 2021 to EUR 3.3 million in 2023–2025, alongside increases from EUR 13.934 million to EUR 30.835 million for Kazakhstan and from EUR 1.319 million to EUR 4.496 million for Armenia. Product-specific export growth exceeded total-export growth in both focal destinations, by 14.1 index points in Kazakhstan and 74.2 index points in Armenia. The package also reproduces the pre-event diagnostic, late-2021 contrast, alternative normalizations, product and comparison-set checks, alternative windows, destination distribution, and descriptive policy-milestone summaries. These results are descriptive and corroborative. They do not identify onward shipment, circumvention, ultimate buyers or end users, enforcement effectiveness, or causal policy effects. The archived product-specific and total-export series come from different Eurostat data vintages, and the broad comparison is interpreted accordingly. Run the complete analysis from the extracted package directory with one command: python3 reproduce.py This deposit is associated with the results package at https://zenodo.org/records/19206576 that supports former version of the article.
title: Governing the Eurasian Roundabout: Anti-Circumvention Governance and Post-Soviet Intermediaries after 2022. V2

summary: 🌟 Summary Ultralytics 8.4.148 makes SAM 3.1 image prediction checkpoints load correctly, enabling reliable point, box, text, and exemplar-based segmentation. 🎯 📊 Key Changes SAM 3.1 checkpoint support 🧠 Added checkpoint-key mapping so sam3.1_multiplex.pt works correctly with SAM and SAM3Predictor . Fixes an issue where SAM 3.1's prompt encoder, mask decoder, embedding, and neck could be silently initialized with random weights. Existing sam3.pt checkpoints remain compatible; the key mapping is effectively a no-op for SAM 3. Supported SAM 3.1 prediction workflows 🖼️ Point and box prompts through SAM and SAM3Predictor . Text and image-exemplar prompts through SAM3SemanticPredictor . SAM 3.1 video tracking with the new Object Multiplex memory architecture is not yet ported . Use the original sam3.pt with the SAM 3 video predictors for video workflows. Documentation updates 📚 Added SAM 3.1 guidance, supported scope, benchmark comparisons, and gated-weight download instructions. Updated the model index to list sam3.1_multiplex.pt . Repository guidance improvements 🛠️ Streamlined the root AGENTS.md and moved documentation-specific instructions into a new docs/AGENTS.md . Preserved important development, testing, release, and implementation-boundary guidance while reducing duplicated repository walkthroughs. Version update 📦 Bumped the package version from 8.4.147 to 8.4.148 . 🎯 Purpose & Impact ✅ Correct segmentation results: SAM 3.1 image predictors now use the trained checkpoint components instead of silently falling back to randomly initialized prompt-processing layers. 🚀 Easier SAM 3.1 adoption: Users can load the new checkpoint through the existing Ultralytics SAM interfaces with minimal workflow changes. 🔍 Clearer expectations: Documentation distinguishes supported SAM 3.1 image prediction from unsupported Object Multiplex video tracking. 🔐 Access requirement: SAM 3.1 weights remain gated by Meta and must be obtained from the approved SAM 3.1 model page on Hugging Face . 👩‍💻 Improved contributor experience: More focused agent guidance makes repository development instructions easier to discover without changing end-user model behavior. summary: Electric vehicles (EVs) experience significant  driving  range degradation in low ambient temperature conditions, primarily due to the elevated energy demand of heating system.  T his paper proposes  an optimal  control strategy for a  positive temperature coefficient ( PTC )  heater-based electric minibus  heating system ,  which is  aimed to  exploit actuators’ redundancy for  energy consumption  minimization  and driving range extension . The strategy  optimally  allocates  control inputs  of multiple actuators  to  provide  heating power demand ed  by a superimposed proportional-integral (PI)  feedback  controller of the  passenger  cabin air temperatur e .  The  optimal  allocation maps prescri be  coolant pump flow, blower air   flow, and inlet air temperature references , and they  are obtained by comprehensive simulations of a high-fidelity multi-physics heating system model over a wide range of quasi-stationary operating conditions .   A low-level PI controller is further designed for the full ,  allocation-related range of operating points to track the  allocated  inlet air temperature reference, while commanding the PTC heater power.   The overall control strategy is validated through co-simulation with a high-fidelity vehicle model  in comparison with an industry baseline strategy , demonstrating a considerable energy consumption reduction in both quasi-stationary and transient (heat up) conditions, as well as improved control performance in terms of shorter heat up intervals.
title: Optimal Control Allocation Strategy for an Energy-efficient PTC Heater-based Electric Vehicle Passenger Cabin Heating System

summary: Abstract Background  Thyroid dysfunction is one of the most common endocrine disorders affecting metabolic activity, psychological well-being, and gastrointestinal function.(1,2) Patients frequently experience elevated thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) levels, stress, bloating, impaired digestion, reduced metabolic efficiency, and decreased quality of life. Although conventional treatment effectively restores thyroid hormone balance in many patients, complementary therapeutic interventions are increasingly being explored to improve overall clinical outcomes and patient-reported health status.  Aim  To evaluate the effect of a Teacurry Thyro Herb Tea for Thyroid on thyroid function, perceived stress, gastrointestinal symptoms, and participant-reported global improvement among adults with thyroid dysfunction.  Materials and Methods:  A prospective, single-arm interventional clinical study was conducted involving  22 adult participants  diagnosed with thyroid dysfunction. Baseline demographic characteristics including age, body weight, height, and body mass index (BMI) were recorded. Clinical assessments included serum thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), perceived stress score (0–40 scale), gastrointestinal symptoms related to bloating, digestion, and metabolism, and Participant Global Impression of Change (PGIC). All parameters were assessed before and after the intervention. The composition of the study formulation will be described separately. Statistical analysis was performed using appropriate descriptive and inferential statistical methods, and statistical significance was considered at  p  < 0.05.  Results:  The intervention demonstrated an overall improvement in multiple clinical outcomes. Mean serum TSH decreased from  10.27 to 3.77 mIU/L , while mean perceived stress scores decreased from  20.45 to 13.18 . Improvement in gastrointestinal symptoms and PGIC scores was observed in the majority of participants. Perceived stress scores decreased in a substantial proportion of participants, indicating improvement in psychological well-being. Gastrointestinal symptoms such as bloating and impaired digestion improved from mild or moderate severity to normal or minimal symptoms in the majority of cases. Participant-reported outcomes also demonstrated favorable changes, with PGIC scores increasing in most participants, suggesting meaningful overall clinical improvement. The intervention was generally well tolerated, and no serious adverse events were documented during the study period.  Conclusion:  The findings of this prospective clinical study suggest that the investigated Teacurry Thyro Herb Tea for Thyroid may contribute to improved thyroid function, reduction in perceived stress, better gastrointestinal health, and enhanced patient-reported quality of life in adults with thyroid dysfunction. These preliminary findings support the potential role of the formulation as a complementary therapeutic option. Larger randomized controlled clinical trials with extended follow-up are warranted to confirm these observations and establish long-term efficacy and safety.   Keywords: Thyroid Dysfunction; Thyroid Stimulating Hormone; TSH; Teacurry Thyro Herb Tea for Thyroid; Teacurry Thyroid Tea; Teacurry; Thyroid Tea; Herbal Tea for Thyroid; Complementary ##plugin
title: Effect of a Plant-Based Herbal Tea Formulation "Teacurry Thyro Herb Tea for Thyroid" on Thyroid Function, TSH Levels, Gastrointestinal Symptoms and Participant-Reported Global Improvement in Adults with Thyroid Dysfunction: Real-World Evidence Clinical Study

summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. Version numbers allow researchers to confirm their data has all been processed in a compati

summary: L'Ange des projections lumineuses was a monthly journal published for the Œuvre des projections catéchistiques of Champtercier (Basses-Alpes), printed at Lyon, and edited by the abbé Georges Aillaud. It ran from 15 October 1902 to 15 September 1903 as the organ of a subscription lending library that circulated magic-lantern slide sets to village clergy, together with the technical advice, lecture texts and equipment notices needed to use them. This deposit is a complete transcription of the ten issues held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France — 198 pages. Numbers 10 and 11, July and August 1903, are absent from the BnF holdings and no copies have been located elsewhere. The journal documents a working provincial distribution network at the moment cinema was arriving in rural France: it lists the slide sets in circulation and their prices, reports what was shown and where, argues over illuminants and apparatus, and by its final number is advertising a cinematograph alongside the lantern equipment. Its technical columns are a detailed record of alcohol, Auer and acetylene illumination in non-commercial exhibition. Method. The text was read from the BnF's page images by a vision language model working on overlapping half-page tiles, without optical character recognition, and then compared word by word by machine against the BnF's own OCR text layer wherever one exists. 1,864 disagreements were found across the 150 pages with a text layer, classified automatically, and checked selectively — not exhaustively — against the page images; eight readings were corrected as a result, and a separate audit for digital artefacts produced a further fifty. Every correction is logged with its evidence. This is machine transcription with editorial checking: it has not been proofread cover to cover against the original and should not be described as though it had. The February, March and April 1903 issues have no BnF text layer, rest on a single reading, and are identified as such. Spelling, accentuation, capitalisation and punctuation follow the page, including where the printing is inconsistent with itself. Contents of this deposit. The reading edition as PDF (119 pp.) and as plain UTF-8 text, both carrying the editorial note as front matter; the per-page source files, which preserve the printed line breaks and their end-of-line hyphens, with the flags raised on each page and a separate folder for the eighteen non-journal leaves; the editorial note; an apparatus of 137 unresolved or adjudicated readings; the full correction log; and the complete uncurated production log, labelled as provenance documentation rather than an apparatus. See README.md. Source. Bibliothèque nationale de France, shelfmark D-72088 (BIS); ISSN 2273-6220; BnF catalogue record cb326930724. Page images: Source gallica.bnf.fr / Bibliothèque nationale de France . Rights. The journal text is in the public domain. The editorial note, annotations, arrangement and other original editorial contributions are licensed under CC BY 4.0 . No copyright is asserted over the underlying public-domain text. Related. A prose introduction to the journal — its publisher, the slide network it served, and its bearing on the arrival of cinema in provincial France — was published at the time of this deposit at billlefurgy.com/ange-des-projections-lumineuses . It is not part of this deposit and is not covered by the method statement above.

summary: Per-pixel  active-flame  image–mask chips from  Sentinel-2  covering  25 large California wildfires  (acquisitions spanning 2020–2026). The deposit contains  2,148  co-registered pairs of false-colour composites and segmentation masks. Each chip is  512 × 512 pixels at 20 m  (~10.24 km across), rendered as a fixed-stretch RGB composite ( R = B12 / SWIR2 ,  G = B11 / SWIR1 ,  B = B8A / NIR ) so flaming combustion is separable from cloud, smoke, fresh char, and bright reflective surfaces. Masks were generated automatically with a  modified HOTMAP SWIR hotspot rule  (confirmed flame where B12 and B12/B8A exceed conservative thresholds, plus a connected growth tier for cooler front margins). Pixel values are  0 = background ,  1 = active fire , and  255 = no-data  (outside the acquisition footprint). The corpus uses a  leak-free fire holdout : whole incidents are assigned to partitions ( 18 train / 3 validation / 4 test ), so evaluation measures transfer to unseen fires rather than random chips from the same landscape. This archive includes: images/  and  masks/  (2,148 PNG files each) summary.csv  (chip-level metadata) partitions.csv  (fire → split assignment) analyst_review/hand_masks/  ( 233  independently reviewed test chips;  54%  of the test split), for quantifying weak-label agreement at chip/cluster level Companion  code , labelling protocol, baseline training scripts, and manuscript figures are available at:   https://github.com/MohammadrezaNarimaniUCDavis/California_Sentinel2_Active_Fire_Dataset This dataset supports a data article prepared for submission to  Data in Brief (Elsevier).

summary: CHAPTER 15 --- Recension- CDJ Opinion 2026‑27 on Judicial Impartiality and Private Affiliations --- The Collège de déontologie des magistrats de l’ordre judiciaire (CDJ) issued Opinion 2026‑27 on 9 June 2026, clarifying when a judge’s membership in an irregular fraternity (and, by extension, other private associations) is compatible with judicial ethics.   The opinion does not impose an absolute ban, but it establishes a principled, appearance‑based test that elevates objective impartiality and procedural safeguards over formal neutrality toward associative life. --- Context and legal background --- The opinion sits within a broader jurisprudential movement that treats impartiality—especially its objective dimension—as a cardinal requirement of a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR).   European and domestic case law increasingly hold that disqualification may be required where circumstances would give a reasonable, fully informed observer legitimate doubts about a judge’s neutrality, even absent proof of actual bias.  The CDJ’s reasoning mirrors this “appearance of impropriety” standard: what matters is whether the private commitment can plausibly be seen as creating a priority allegiance or solidarity that conflicts with the judicial duty of independence and neutrality. ---  Core holding: conditional incompatibility --- The CDJ frames its answer in two branches: - Incompatibility: Membership is incompatible with judicial deontological obligations when the Masonic oath induces a “prior allegiance or solidarity” that could override judicial duties. - Compatibility with reservations: Where no such prior allegiance is established, membership remains possible but is surrounded by “important reservations” and requires heightened vigilance to ensure independence, impartiality, and neutrality in both fact and appearance. The opinion explicitly links this risk to three structural features often associated with Masonic practice: an oath of allegiance, an obligation of secrecy, and inter‑member solidarity—each of which can undermine public confidence in the judge’s neutrality. ---  The invisibility problem and informational asymmetry --- A distinctive contribution of the opinion is its focus on invisibility. Unlike family ties, professional networks, or financial interests, Masonic membership is typically not verifiable by litigants.  This informational asymmetry prevents parties from invoking standard procedural safeguards (e.g., recusal motions grounded in disclosed relationships), thereby magnifying the appearance risk.   The CDJ effectively treats non‑disclosable affiliations that entail strong internal loyalties as structurally suspect, because they remove the very mechanism—transparency—that allows objective impartiality to be tested and preserved. --- Constitutional and convention tensions --- While the opinion builds on existing case law, it surfaces unresolved tensions with fundamental rights: - Freedom of association and conscience: Judges retain associative rights, and any limitation must be proportionate and necessary in a democratic society.  - Proportionality and legal certainty: Because the CDJ’s opinions are not binding law and cannot by themselves create statutory incompatibilities, the practical force of the guidance relies on its authority and on how disciplinary bodies and courts receive it. These tensions suggest that a future constitutional or convention‑based challenge could refine the balance between associative freedom and the functional requirements of judicial office. ---- Practical implications for judges --- In the interim, judges face a delicate choice: - Seek prior guidance: Given the opinion’s authority, prudent practice is to consult the CDJ (or equivalent ethics bodies) before joining any association whos

summary: 2.2.0 A minor version, not a patch: the change below alters what a default run leaves on disk. Nothing about your results, final outputs or logs changes, but a default that deletes files users previously got to keep is more than a patch. Changed Intermediate pfiles are now deleted as the run progresses, at defaults. Each QC step reads a genotype file and writes a new one — callrate reads your input and writes …_callrate , sex reads that and writes …_sex , and so on — so a ten-step run creates ten copies of your data. At GP2 release scale each copy is tens of GiB. Cleanup used to be skipped whenever warn_only was set, and warn-and-continue is the default , so at defaults every copy survived for the whole run. The only way to reclaim the disk was --no-warn , which also turns warn-and-continue into fail-fast — so you could not have both. That is a bad trade on a long run, where warn-and-continue exists precisely so an eight-hour job does not die on one recoverable step. The two flags no longer interfere: | | before | now | |---|---|---| | (default) | keeps every copy | deletes each copy once the next is written | | --full-output | keeps every copy | keeps every copy | | --no-warn | deletes + fail-fast | fail-fast only | | --no-warn --full-output | keeps + fail-fast | keeps + fail-fast | --full-output is now the only switch governing retention; --no-warn is purely failure policy. Peak disk during a run drops from roughly one working copy per step to one overall — on the round-19 full-GP2 run, ~98 GiB written against a ~50 GiB peak. If you relied on the old default to inspect intermediates, pass --full-output — it reproduces the previous behavior exactly. A failed step's input is still kept either way, so a broken run can still be examined.
title: GenoTools

summary: The Earth That Heard is not presented as a literary reconstruction built around biblical verses. It records a textual architecture that the author argues is already present in the Torah itself — a structure that emerged through fifteen years of research into Biblical Hebrew morphology, roots, recurring letter patterns, and the internal organization of the text. The essay traces a continuous thread from the murder of Abel in Genesis to Joshua’s altar on Mount Ebal. Motifs that initially appear independent — earth and blood, firstfruit and firstborn, field and El Shaddai, rising and place, sacrifice, Shechem, the opening of the earth, and the return of the firstfruits — progressively converge into a single narrative structure. The central proposal is that Abel’s unfinished offering, Cain’s failure, and the wounded earth are not abandoned episodes: their resolution unfolds across the Torah and reaches completion in Joshua. The work explicitly separates three epistemic levels: Text — what the biblical text states; Reading — what emerges when distant passages are compared; and Implication — the larger interpretation suggested by the resulting structure. The pattern is also tested quantitatively. The present essay contains 136 key verses; the original connection-density test was performed on a pre-set group of 124 verses selected by the narrative. Using the Control Alphabet / Mandatory Root morphology developed in The Road and the Place , the observed network produced Z = 19.37 (p < 0.0002) against 5,000 random permutations. A second, deliberately simpler test removes the seven control letters א, מ, ת, נ, י, ה, ו from every word and performs direct string matching with no root database; it still yields Z = 10.29 (p < 0.0002) , with the same major long-range connections rising to the top. A raw-word test remains significant at Z = 5.17 (p = 0.0013) . A separate anthology comparison tests whether similarly chosen biblical themes automatically generate the same effect. The Ebal/Shechem axis reaches Z = 17.35 , compared with Covenant Z = 10.07 , Jerusalem/Temple Z = 1.60 , Joseph Z = −8.13 , and Tabernacle Z = −7.16 . The result does not statistically prove the theological interpretation; it shows that the textual concentration being interpreted is itself measurable and unusual. A scientific appendix further examines comparative anatomical and genomic parallels associated with one of the essay’s most unexpected motifs, while explicitly distinguishing scientific observation from midrashic interpretation. After fifteen years of work, the author does not regard this as a story invented to fit the text, but as part of a larger architecture that the text itself gradually disclosed — a structure he considers himself fortunate to have uncovered, even if only in part, and to place on record now. Bilingual publication: Hebrew original and English edition.
title: The Earth That Listened — The Hidden Timeline from Genesis to Joshua

summary: Automated risk decisions increasingly depend on probabilistic assessments transmitted across organisational and computational boundaries. A probability estimate may remain numerically intact while losing the contextual information required to evaluate its evidentiary dependence — a condition we term Provenance Loss . We introduce Orphaned Inference — a probabilistic output P ( H | E ) that propagates downstream after its contextual qualification is stripped at a transmission boundary — and show that when downstream agents continue scalar-posterior updating using marginal likelihood ratios, the resulting propagation is equivalent to a Na ̈ıve-Bayes-style independence approximation over the correlated evidence sequence. This double-counts the shared environmental signal, producing Directional Context Amplification , quantified by the Cumulative Provenance Amplification (CPA n ) metric. Under environmental context drift ( C 0 → C 1 ), accumulated phantom certainty persists into the post-shift regime as Post-Shift Epistemic Persistence , driving the mean absolute posterior error close to 1 in true-negative states ( H = 0) during the pre-shift period. In risk-analysis terms, provenance loss separates the numerical value of a risk estimate from the evidentiary conditions under which it remains decision-valid: downstream decision makers may receive an apparently precise probability whose effective evidentiary weight is substantially overstated. A Monte Carlo simulation ( N = 5 , 000 trials, n = 15 agent chain) demonstrates the predicted cascade under the specified parameter regime and documents monotone growth of CPA n across sampled correlation values ρ ∈ { 0 , . . . , 0 . 8 } . We propose three provenance-aware risk-control safeguards and discuss their governance trade-offs.

summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. summary: This repository contains two LC–MS/MS raw data files (and .mgf versions if needed), associated search parameters, and curated FASTA databases generated from purified fibrinogen clots crosslinked by endogenous FXIIIa or recombinant transglutaminase 2 (TG2). These samples represent a controlled benchmark system for evaluating crosslink-mass spectrometry (XL-MS) software performance on non-cleavable enzymatic Q–K isopeptide bonds. Unlike conventional chemical crosslinkers, these transglutaminase-mediated crosslinks are zero-length modifications formed by ammonia (NH₃) loss, creating unique challenges for false discovery control and site assignment. The datasets are provided to enable transparent, community-driven comparison of XL search engines and to advance methodological development in enzymatic crosslink identification.
title: Open Benchmark Dataset for Enzymatic Q–K Crosslink Identification by LC–MS/MS

summary: A hydro cascade system benchmark for comparing short-term scheduling methods Frontier Falls is an eight-reservoir hydropower cascade with hourly hydrologic and electricity-market forcing, packaged as a fully specified benchmark problem. Its structure is inspired by the Cumberland River reservoir system, but all names, parameters, and operating assumptions have been modified for benchmark use —  nothing in this dataset represents actual reservoir operations, and all inflows are synthetic . Prices are public market data published by ISO New England (see  License ). The benchmark supports hydropower day-ahead scheduling studies with common physical system and shared forcing scenarios. Use cases include: Scheduling optimization  — comparing algorithms (MPC, SDDP, MILP, heuristics) on an identical, reproducible problem. Model coupling  — workflows that couple river-operations models with power-dispatch optimization. AI-agent operations  — LLM agents making bidding and release decisions with tool support. Total installed capacity: 853 MW across four storage projects and four mainstem run-of-river-style projects in a multi-river network. Detailed cascade system specifications are accompanied by five hydrologic scenarios (with 31-member ensemble 168-hour reforecasts) and five market scenarios that include day-ahead real-time (DA-RT) prices and associated reforecasts. See README.md for further details. Citing Frontier Falls Turner, S., Yu, A., Feng, J. Z., Ploussard, Q., Pavičević, M., & Galelli, S. (2026).  Frontier Falls  (version 0.9.0) [Data set]. Zenodo.  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22680552 Machine-readable metadata is in CITATION.cff . License Except for the underlying ISO New England price values (see below), this dataset and its documentation are released under the  Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0) . You are free to share and adapt the material for any purpose, including commercially, provided you give appropriate credit (see  Citing Frontier Falls ). The full legal text is in  LICENSE . The companion simulator code (GitLab) is licensed separately; see that repository. Market price data Price data in this dataset are public market data published by ISO New England Inc. ( https://www.iso-ne.com ) through ISO Express, covering 2020-10-05 through 2025-10-05 (one source year per market scenario; each  Forcing/market/MS-*/metadata.json  gives the window and calendar mapping). Locational marginal prices are classified as Public Market Information under Section 3.0(a) of the ISO New England Information Policy (Tariff Attachment D). ISO-NE provides these data "as is" and has not reviewed or endorsed this dataset. Any use of this dataset must cite ISO New England Inc. as the original data source. The curation, derived fields, documentation, and code in this record are released under CC BY 4.0 ( https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ ). The authors claim no rights in the underlying price values. Users are responsible for their own compliance with ISO-NE's website terms and conditions ( https://www.iso-ne.com/legal-privacy ).
